entries.title: Lonnie Bunch Is Leaving the Smithsonian
entries.summary: After months of clashes with the White House, the historian and leader of the institution is retiring later this year.
entries.content:
After months of clashes with the White House, the historian and leader of the institution is retiring later this year.

Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch plans to announce his retirement from the institution at the end of this year, bringing to a close a tenure marked by unprecedented pressure on the museum complex from a White House keen on controlling how to tell the nation’s history. A person with knowledge of the situation confirmed the departure to The Atlantic.

Bunch’s exit will leave the Smithsonian, which is partially federally funded, with a vacuum at the top as it faces escalating efforts from the Trump administration to influence its work. Bunch, known to be diplomatic and evenhanded, had largely staved off the White House’s encroachment over a tumultuous 18 months in which the Trump administration issued executive orders and memos criticizing the museums and threatened to withhold funding. Most recently, President Trump signed an executive order calling for signage to be added to the exterior of the National Museum of American History warning about what the administration believes is an inaccurate and partisan telling of history.

Before becoming secretary, Bunch was best known as the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

entries.title: The Novel That Looks Death in the Eye
entries.summary: Emma Cline’s Switzy might not make readers happy, but it could strike them with moments of sublime clarity.
entries.content:
Emma Cline’s Switzy might not make readers happy, but it could strike them with moments of sublime clarity.

The human brain has a method for dealing with the intrinsic fear of death. Terror-management theory, which builds on the work of the cultural anthropologist Ernest Becker, explains that the psyche handles this fear in a variety of ways. Many people either escape reality or adopt a belief system that promises immortality: so on the one hand, sex, drugs, or entertainment; on the other, religion, fame, or careerism. Or we might immerse ourselves in family, or culture—something that imbues life with meaning. Otherwise, the theory goes, we would be cognitively immobilized by impending doom.

In her gut-twisting third novel, Switzy, Emma Cline does not abide by the tenets of terror management. Instead, she pulls death out from behind the curtain and forces her readers to look it in the eye for more than 300 pages. Switzy follows the final few days in the life of David Hastings, a former high-flying executive who’s been forced into retirement, and obsolescence, by an Alzheimer’s diagnosis. He has taken advantage of Switzerland’s right-to-die laws, paying the fees (a paltry sum for a wealthy man) and filling out the required paperwork. Now he’ll swallow some barbiturates and die in an impersonal room just outside Zurich, far from his family and his home in America. Cline’s approach is merciless—not toward David, for whom she shows tenderness and grace, but toward the reader, who will be nearly flattened by this novel. Or so I sincerely hope, because death ought to flatten us once in a while.

Switzy begins mid-flight, as David hurtles across the Atlantic in a friend’s private jet. Accompanied by Cody—a former corporate underling who now functions as David’s caretaker, body man, and secretary—he lands first in London. There, he has dinner with his only child, an emotionally distant daughter who doesn’t know about her father’s decline, let alone his upcoming euthanasia. David tours a museum, visits his grandson, reboards the plane for his final flight, to Zurich; he dazedly lets Cody steer him around as a parent would guide a toddler. The younger man negotiates the intricacies of the world on David’s behalf, buffering him from the demands of day-to-day life—buying a museum ticket, sending a text message, procuring beverages.

David needs the help: He is at times absent in his own mind. As rendered by Cline in a wandering, dreamlike style, this becomes a startling and eerie phenomenon—like the moment you realize you’ve been driving for miles but don’t recall anything about the journey. Far from experiencing the blissful ignorance that some people might project onto dementia patients, David is all too aware that his brain has locked away basic memories and social customs. He writes his grandson’s name, Rainer, in a notebook so he can recall it; a clock “in big kindergarten letters” informs him of the date and time each morning; he stares too long at someone in the museum and provokes his annoyance. And he sees each gap, knows that it signals another loss. “Work,” he thinks as he chews a croissant, “everything seemed like work. Even these good things—even this buttered mouthful.”

The first half of Switzy crawls by, but it feels achingly necessary. This is time the way David experiences it, slowed down and sometimes skipped over: Alzheimer’s novels are rare, and those told from the patient’s point of view are even rarer. Cline, always a graceful stylist, employs a kind of abbreviated modernism to leap among David’s thoughts. They skitter backwards to memories of his failed marriage and his time at a boys’ boarding school. They run in circles, around catchy sayings—such as a mnemonic about Henry VIII’s abbreviated marriages, “Divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived”—that Alzheimer’s hasn’t stolen from him. And they jump ahead to the moment and manner of his death, which inches closer with every turned page.

Cline’s last novel, The Guest, also followed a character who hastily approaches a reckoning. Alex, a poor and wily 22-year-old sex worker who has just been kicked out of the home of her most recent catch, Simon, has to make it through five days in the Hamptons, until she can plead to be let back into the high-end milieu of Simon’s Labor Day party. Dead-eyed and mutable, Alex, like David, is trying to put on just enough of a show to pass muster with the people around her. For her, a different kind of death awaits—complete impoverishment, and removal from a perch where she may or may not belong.

Switzy raises the stakes on this kind of quest. As the novel’s second half picks up steam, so does the cadence of David’s confrontations with the fact of his looming extinction. When the plane lands in Zurich, an official comes on to inspect their passports. “David smiled to himself. It was obvious, wasn’t it? This man was Death. Why else would he know to come right onboard?” Soon after, he sees Death again as a waiter, a busboy, two restaurant patrons. On his last night, he wakes repeatedly in his hotel, checking the sky’s brightness as a sign of how much time he has left. An Omega watch advertisement catches his eye, and though he doesn’t say it, the meaning is clear: Omega is the last letter in the Greek alphabet, the universal symbol of finality.

As long as David cannot stop returning to his ticking clock, neither can you. This kind of sustained attention to the one topic many people spend their lives avoiding is practically subversive—a thrill, really. And it’s possibly a public service too. Studies have repeatedly shown that people who think about death on a regular basis are happier, because contemplating mortality reinforces the idea, as Emily Dickinson put it, “That it will never come again/ Is what makes life so sweet.” I daresay most readers won’t feel much happiness reading Switzy—though it does have glimmers of humor—but they might experience moments of sublime clarity.

Death functions here in a way that isn’t common in fiction. Its presence doesn’t make this novel a tearjerker—it’s not, for example, Maggie O’Farrell’s Hamnet, which beautifully laments the loss of a child. It offers no spectacle akin to Anne Boleyn’s trembling march to the scaffold at the end of Hilary Mantel’s singular historical novel, Bring Up the Bodies. Unlike many 19th-century novels, Switzy doesn’t use death to solve a social problem, à la Anna Karenina (romantic devastation) and Madame Bovary (financial ruin). Nor is death here a handy plot device, as it is in so many works across the past century. Switzy is not about the living who are left behind. Cline’s approach to death marks different territory: It’s about raw, undeniable truth.

Dying is a transformative event: People pass from the only reality they’ve ever been able to recognize into something nebulous and ungraspable (even for the most fervent religious believers). And this might sound obvious, but you, reader, will die. So will I. Much of humanity has raised its defenses high against death, perhaps unintentionally, as Ernest Becker proposes. So how will it feel to see a man marching straight toward it—not unflinchingly, or tremulously, but with a perfectly ordinary mixture of confusion and acceptance?

In Switzy’s final pages, David becomes a man who cannot help but be alive, even in his last moments. He doesn’t want to eat breakfast, but he feels it’s “better to have something in the stomach.” He feels irritated that he is given a blue pen to sign documents—“blue ink was for grocery lists.” He fumbles over his last words. Cline writes, “His was both the realest life in the room and the most unreal.” The line between everything and nothing is as thin as a breath of air.

entries.title: The Myth of Perfect Knowledge
entries.summary: Science will never be able to give a completely objective description of the world. That should make us humbler—and wiser.
entries.content:
Science will never be able to give a completely objective description of the world. That should make us humbler—and wiser.

The modern world owes a lot to the Enlightenment, the 18th-century intellectual movement that emphasized the power of reason. But the Enlightenment also created a myth: that we can get to know the objective world completely, with total clarity, as if we were looking at it from the outside. This myth is challenged by the Enlightenment’s greatest legacy—modern science.

Reality is more complex than we expected. Physics—my trade, and perhaps the most objective among the sciences—questions the possibility of a full description of how things objectively are. An electron can be in a “quantum superposition,” so that to an observer, it doesn’t occupy just one location—and so can you, my reader. This does not mean that you could perceive being dislocated between two positions; as perceived by yourself, you are always in just one place. But an object’s properties may differ depending on who, or what, is looking at them—or may not even be defined at all. Properties are not simple features of things: They are relations between one thing and another. What we call “the world” is therefore only how some parts of reality manifest themselves to other parts—us, for instance.

Humanity has always been aware that our understanding is partial and biased. But the fact that an objective and knowable reality is incompatible with the grammar of physics is astonishing. The Enlightenment could consider the mind as being outside the world, in an abstract realm of reason where knowledge resides. But human minds are not outside reality, watching it from its exterior. We, like everything else, are part of the very nature we study.

Our knowledge is only one example of the many correlations that intertwine different parts of nature. In the early 20th century, Niels Bohr, a founder of quantum theory, realized that quantum phenomena indicate that we cannot discard our own physical nature when we observe the world. The ideal of grasping objective reality by making the observer irrelevant is incompatible with physics. We are quantum processes interacting with other quantum processes. Our knowledge is a rich but incomplete set of correlations between one piece of the world–ourselves–and the rest of it.

To see this fact from another point of view, consider saying “It’s raining and Ann does not know it.” This makes sense: You know that it’s raining and that Ann doesn’t. But if you replace “Ann” with a first-person pronoun, the result is odd: “It’s raining and I do not know it.” How can you declare that it’s raining if you do not know it? This observation points to the fact that every proposition can only express the knowledge of the speaker or writer. No proposition is asserted from outside reality, because there is nothing outside reality. To say “It is raining” is really to say: “I, as part of reality, know that it’s raining.” Objective statements independent of any knower are fictions. Purely objective reality is a useful myth, but only a myth. Anything said about the state of the world comes from someone’s singular perspective.

This means that all of our knowledge is intrinsically uncertain. All statements have unavoidable margins of uncertainty. Indeed, we can be wrong about anything, even the basic facts of our own lives. My father grew up sure that his first name was Franco until he asked for a copy of his birth certificate and found out that my grandfather, without telling my grandma, had registered him as Giulio. He had been wrong about his own name. Humanity has been collectively wrong over and over again. We thought the sun moved around the earth, then learned that it is the earth that orbits the sun. Great scientists are even more likely to be wrong than others, because they have the courage to try—Einstein’s published work includes many mistakes.

But in science, as in daily life, we do not need certainty; being reasonably sure is good enough. If I have an airplane to catch, I will go to the airport even though I’m not totally sure that the flight will take off; if I waited for certainty, I’d never leave home. Modern science offers an enormous body of knowledge that is effective and, in many domains, far better than all the alternatives, but it gives us no absolute certainty, no ultimate story, no Truth with a capital T.

Within science, there are different ways of describing the same things. A glass of water can be described in terms of physics (its mass, velocity), thermodynamics (its temperature), chemistry (there is more than just H2O in any glass of water), biology (bacteria swim in it), particle physics (its electrons, protons, and neutrons), psychology (“Why did I fill the glass?”), economics (its price), and more. Each account is valid in its own terms; each reflects a way in which the same object interacts with different parts of reality, from atoms to the global economy. But none exhausts an “ultimate truth” of the glass.

The same is true for human beings. I can think of you, my reader, as a body, as a mind, or as a soul. These aren’t different entities: They are the same entity, described in different languages, using different conceptual schemes, focusing on different aspects of the same you and different ways in which you interact with other parts of reality. There is no sharp separation or metaphysical gap between body and soul; matter and spirit; the physical world and the world of laws, ideas, and norms.

In this sense, all things are equal: They are all aspects of the same natural world, considered from different perspectives, none of which is the ultimate one. Everything can be considered fundamental from one perspective or another. The expression “the equality of all things” comes from the title of the second chapter of The Book of Zhuangzi, one of the greatest books of humankind—an ancient classic of Chinese philosophy that articulates a similar intriguing perspectival and anti-foundational naturalism.

This is the view to which I think modern science leads us. Many people resist it, some out of fear of losing solid reference points: objectivity, certainties, absolute morality, an immortal soul. But scientific knowledge does not become less valuable if you remain open to doubt. Morality does not lose power if you recognize that it is rooted in our biology, culture, and history. Our values do not weaken because they are rooted in what we are, not in something outside us. And life is even more beautiful and precious without dreams of immortality. We are not—as French existentialism described us—thrown into alien nature. In nature, we are home.

In fact, it seems to me that recognizing the perspectival aspect of knowledge, values, and beliefs, and of reality itself, could help us become a bit less arrogant, a bit humbler and wiser. Conflicts between individuals or countries don’t stem only from greed and thirst for power. They are also fueled by the belief that we are objectively right and the enemy is objectively wrong, which ignores the plurality of perspectives. We have our values that guide us, but understanding the perspective of others is the first step toward wisdom—and toward peace. In our era of nuclear armaments, ignoring that others have different perspectives, and failing to respect them, could drag the world into a catastrophe.

entries.title: Zoos Are Doubling Down on Very Unnatural Habitats
entries.summary: Could high-tech toys help captive animals act more wild?
entries.content:
Could high-tech toys help captive animals act more wild?

Hudson, a 10-year-old arctic fox at Massachusetts’s Stone Zoo, was not doing all that much when his caretakers came by his enclosure one sunny morning last month. But the moment he detected their approach, he scurried over. His eyes focused on the pink, kibble-filled puzzle box they were holding—a programmable, lab-made device that’s part of an experiment in letting captive animals play around with technology.

In the past year, in partnership with a team led by Rébecca Kleinberger, an engineer and a computer scientist at Northeastern University, Stone Zoo has introduced Hudson to his puzzle feeder, two black bears to a motion-sensitive bubble machine, a family of colobus monkeys to an interactive cabinet of mirrors, and more. The zoo is not alone in its tech curiosity. At the Maryland Zoo, caretakers have debuted a hunting simulation for polar bears, in which a robot arm extends and retracts a romaine leaf smeared with peanut butter—mimicking a prey animal poking its head out of an ice hole. At Zoo Atlanta, keepers have partnered with engineers at the Georgia Institute of Technology to develop an interactive audio wall where elephants can insert their trunks into motion-sensitive holes to trigger a variety of low-frequency sounds. At some facilities, penguins have been given access to iPad games designed for pet cats, and orangutans have been taught to play on an Xbox.

Hudson the arctic fox makes a case for the benefits that captive animals can derive from tech. His quarters at the zoo, where he lives alone, offer few of the thrills he’d experience in the wild—chasing after live rodents and birds, wooing mates, fleeing wolves and bears. In the past, when I’d come to his enclosure as a visitor to the zoo, he had always been snoozing; simpler toys rarely captured his attention for more than a few minutes at a time, his keepers told me. This time, he trotted. He sniffed. He wriggled his tail. He reared up on his hind legs and used his long-clawed front paws to spin the pink wheel of his puzzle counterclockwise, then clockwise, until it yielded crunchy bits of kibble.

When Kleinberger’s team first approached Pete Costello, the assistant curator at Stone Zoo, and his colleagues about the prospect of introducing the zoo’s residents to technology, his mind swam with images of creatures clutching iPads, doomscrolling their days away, he told me. But as Hudson spun his box—which can be toggled up and down through four levels of difficulty and programmed to release food at set intervals—I glanced over at Costello and the other keepers. They were beaming like proud parents and complimenting the fox’s deft moves: Ooh, good spin … Yup, he’s got it right away!

Regardless of how well wild animals are cared for in captivity, their lives by definition shrink. In enclosures, removed from nature’s shifting circumstances and perils, and, often, the company of their own kind, they “lead very impoverished lives,” Clara Mancini, a pioneering researcher in the field of animal-computer interaction at the Open University, in the United Kingdom, told me. Technology may at first seem to make captive animals’ lives more artificial. But it’s starting to look like a good way to coax them into behaving more wildly.

The field of technological enrichment for animals might have taken off decades earlier, Joey Golden, the curator of animal-behavior programs at the Maryland Zoo, told me. In the 1970s and ’80s, for instance, the scientist Hal Markowitz tinkered with devices that taught Diana monkeys to dispense food from a vending machine, or flung “flying meatballs” for servals. The animals were, by all appearances, interested in Markowitz’s devices. But “what he was building,” Golden said, “was incredibly artificial” to others in the research community who were focused on better replicating wild habitats.

Animal-behavior researchers have since come around to the idea that the aesthetics of an animal’s surroundings are less important than how well those surroundings serve them. Creatures need the unpredictability of the natural world; in the monotony of captivity, where humans are in charge, a device that can shift with an animal’s needs can offer that creature “a little more control,” Kleinberger told me. A wobbly chew toy stuffed with a mini meatball might entertain a fox like Hudson for a few minutes. But it can’t operate on a shifting schedule or become more difficult as the user learns its quirks—unlike a teched-up puzzle feeder.

Kleinberger got her start by creating voice-technology tools for musicians and people who stutter. But several years ago, keepers at the San Diego Zoo asked if she would develop a device to help a beats-loving hyacinth macaw named Sampson control his own playlist. Kleinberger was pleased to see not only that the device not only gave Sampson access to the tunes he wanted to hear, but that he’d bob his head along with the music to attract the types of zoo visitors whom he seemed to particularly enjoy. “He really liked children or people wearing red T-shirts,” Kleinberger said. Sampson, in effect, had made the technology his own.

Determining what animals may get out of different technologies requires some guesses and leaps. At Stone Zoo, a pair of black bears, Smoky and Bubba, are certainly interested in the device that Kleinberger’s team built for them—a motion-sensitive machine that blows scented bubbles. The day I visited, both bears lumbered over to the lemon-scented, then bacon-scented bubbles streaming into their enclosure; they took big, huffing whiffs; flicked their ears; and occasionally licked their chops. The bubbles were stimulating the bears’ keen noses, engaging a sense they might not otherwise use very often. But, of course, the bears couldn’t tell us how much they actually liked the experience. When I asked Mancini how researchers know the full effects that technology has on other creatures, her answer was simple: “We don’t.”

Animal behaviorists generally don’t like to use words such as enjoyment and boredom to describe their study subjects. “Those are very human concepts,” Kleinberger said. But if the goal is to improve captive animals’ lives, sentiments at least akin to enjoyment and boredom are what enrichment researchers must try to measure. Scientists are left to use the animals’ actions as a code, Malu Celli, Zoo New England’s vice president of animal care, told me. Researchers look for certain behaviors that they might feel are lacking in captivity: more swimming by a penguin, more walking by a bear, more foraging by a fox. They’ll also pay attention to how a creature’s senses are engaged—whether an animal’s ears lift or its eyes focus on a machine—while watching for subtle signs of distress. A positive result can be as simple as “Do they come back to it?” Kleinberger said. Or, presented with the same system, do they run away?

Engagement doesn’t necessarily mean fulfillment. An animal that’s spending long periods of time with a screen might just be drawn in by the lights. And in the same way that chasing a laser might infuriate a cat who can never catch its blinking red “prey,” touch screens that ask animals to chase virtual objects might never satisfy predatory instincts. Tech might also suck up so much of an animal’s attention that it doesn’t do much of anything else, or engross a group of creatures so much that they begin to compete for access, Marcela Benítez, an animal-behavior researcher at Emory University, told me. At some zoos, in fact, caretakers have entirely banned smartphones around their great-ape enclosures out of concern that the animals might get too much screen time.

Researchers are still trying to understand the extent to which different species can recognize two-dimensional images or videos of themselves or others of their own kind. Certain brainy creatures can be good candidates for screen-based interactions: Kleinberger and her colleagues have had success with a video-chatting system for pet parrots, highly social birds that commonly end up isolated in a human home. Many of the parrots they studied would chatter or sing loudly to each other through the screen. One parrot in the study, Kleinberger said, started flying more often after a series of calls with another bird that frequently flitted about. Some of the parrots, though, just lay down next to the device or fell asleep.

Several of the scientists I spoke with for this story also happened to be parents of very young children; more than once, they compared the types of enrichment they were tinkering with to the games and toys they’d shared with their toddlers, for better or for worse. Some wondered about the potential for addiction, or even about skewing certain creatures’ perception of reality by overloading them with artifice. But projecting too much of humans’ own complicated relationships with technology onto animals can unnecessarily limit research. Just as animals might derive the same benefits that people do, they also might not experience the same harms. With Hudson, Kleinberger at first worried that the fox might become unhealthily obsessed with his puzzle box. But the presence of the device, she said, instead seemed to boost his enthusiasm for activity in general. It’s hard to say for sure, but maybe the technology reminded him that there was still fun to be had inside his artificial world.

entries.title: Voters Have a Message for Democrats
entries.content:
During the early Trump era, focus groups taught me everything about the disconnect between Washington and what voters really care about. An early revelation came in July 2018; I had flown to Columbus, Ohio, to hear from a group of people who’d voted for Donald Trump in 2016, but only reluctantly.

Three days before, Trump had participated in a diplomatic summit in Helsinki with Russian President Vladimir Putin. By that point, the U.S. intelligence community had publicly concluded that Putin had personally ordered a campaign to meddle in the 2016 presidential election for Trump’s direct benefit. At a press conference after their meeting, Trump was asked whether he believed his own intelligence agencies or the Russian president. “President Putin says it’s not Russia,” Trump responded. “I don’t see any reason why it would be.” And just like that, the president had undermined 80 years of American foreign policy, prompting a bipartisan meltdown in Washington.

I was excited to hear what Trump-skeptical voters in the heartland thought about this epochal moment. These were the kinds of people who had been Reagan’s fiercest Cold Warriors, right? Surely they wouldn’t tolerate something like this from the American president. But when the moderator running the focus group asked the participants for their thoughts about Trump’s comments, he got a lot of blank stares.

Even big news like this doesn’t always filter down to voters, so the moderator explained the incident. I figured that once the group understood what had happened, outrage would follow. Nope. One person said that Trump’s comments were “wrong,” but the feeling in the room was that of a collective shrug. The thing we were all freaking out about in D.C. had barely registered out there among the voters.

Since that moment, I’ve conducted more than 400 focus groups with thousands of voters across the political spectrum. To my knowledge, this is the largest and most consistent qualitative study of voter sentiment during the Trump era. Here’s what I’ve learned: People are wild. They are full of contradictions. They lament our deep political divisions while raging about their political enemies. They believe in grace but cut their Trumpy brother out of their life forever. They’re married to an immigrant but voted for the guy who wants to deport millions of people who have the same immigration status as their wife. They hate the government and want to lower the national debt, but they also want the government to spend more to help them and their communities. They call themselves pro-life but believe in a woman’s right to choose. I could go on.

Listening to voters is a cheat code for understanding politics—democracy, after all, is the collective will of the voters—yet few people in politics do it. If you’re running a campaign, you might do a series of focus groups with voters in your district or state. If you’re a politician, you might go on “listening tours,” chat with people at the state fair, or host campaign events. But rarely do politicians and campaigns take the time to talk in-depth about why people feel the way they do.

The reality is, the closer you get to institutional politics, the further you are from the people whom politics and government are supposed to serve. Washington is less a swamp than a bubble, inside of which the rest of America becomes an abstraction.

I’m a former Republican who left the party after Trump took it over. I saw him for what he was: an existential threat to American liberal democracy. So I say this as someone who both crossed the political divide and still feels that Americans are underreacting to the acute threat of Trump and Trumpism: If Democrats want to win back power, they’re going to need to learn how to better relate to the American people, as people.

For all of their nonlinear thinking and idiosyncratic views, voters have told me a couple of things over and over again: They think the system is broken, and they feel that they’ve been lied to in ways that make their life tangibly worse. Fewer of them now believe that if you work hard and play by the rules, you can get ahead in this country. Instead, they think that “establishment” politicians are benefiting from this system while everyone else loses out. Because of that, they want to place their trust in leaders who come across as “real people” who are genuinely interested in improving voters’ day-to-day life—not just winning and holding political office.

In 2016, Republican voters looked at their party’s leadership—the Romneys, McCains, and Bushes—and decided they were done. Those leaders were too weak, too unwilling to fight, too committed to norms and processes that Democrats didn’t respect anyway. Republican voters hired a wrecking ball named Trump to knock it all down. Ten years later, I’m hearing similar sentiments from Democratic voters. They don’t trust Chuck Schumer, Hakeem Jeffries, or any of the old-guard party leaders who allowed Trump to take over America. They want their own wrecking ball.

There’s a distinction here. Democrats don’t want Trump’s politics or even necessarily his all-out norm breaking. But they want his energy. They’re sick of a Democratic Party that does the functional equivalent of sending a strongly worded letter while democracy burns down around us. That tension—absolutely not, but also yes—is the defining mood among Democratic voters right now. They don’t want to become what they hate. But they are tired of losing to it.

I don’t think that most Democratic elites understand this reality. In those circles, the dominant debate seems to be about whether the party should be more progressive or more moderate. The future of the party is seen as a policy question. But when I listen to Democratic voters, they’re not asking for ideological recalibration or even policy specifics. They trust that if the right person makes it into office, the policy questions will take care of themselves. Instead, the Democratic voters I’m listening to are almost universally asking a different question: Why aren’t you fighting harder?

Last year, my team and I decided to run an experiment. We convened a couple of focus groups with Democrats who wanted the party to be more moderate, then a couple with Democrats who wanted the party to be more progressive. If I didn’t tell you which group was which, you would not be able to hear the difference by listening to them.

Here’s a sampling from the more moderate group. Brandon from Georgia lamented that Democrats don’t “fight fire with fire,” saying, “Republicans will take an issue even if it’s completely fake news, and they’ll just beat it down the hatches.” Karen from Pennsylvania said that Jeffries is a “great guy” but that he is “too weak,” and “I think he’s just got to be more forceful, and maybe even nasty.”

Now here are some of the Democrats who want the party to be more progressive. Jeffrey from Georgia: “I mean, the party just seems to me like it’s like a turtle that’s been turned on its back, you know. It’s just kind of flailing around hoping that it could, you know, somehow right itself.” Mary from Michigan said: “Them actually showing a spine would be a delightful change of pace. I have been calling my congresspeople every damn day telling them to not go along with the Cabinet approvals, to not rubber-stamp things just because you’re in the minority. They have not done a single thing.”

These voters didn’t speak in terms of wanting the party to be more to the left or more to the center. They all just wanted Democrats to be more aggressive.

Democratic voters have watched their party lose battles that they thought were already settled—abortion rights, voting rights, basic democratic norms—and they’re done with the old approach. They’ve watched Democratic politicians continue to engage with MAGA Republicans like it’s 2012 and Mitt Romney is running the GOP. Democratic voters recognize that the old rules don’t apply anymore. It’s not clear that their leaders have caught up to that reality.

How can Democrats make a change? One of the things that Trump did—and I mean this not as a value judgment but as a factual matter—was transform the relationship between the president and the public. He made it direct, constant, intimate, and unavoidable. Through his tweets and his rallies and his Fox News call-ins and his Truth Social posts, Trump is in people’s face all the time. You know what he thinks about everything. You know when he sleeps by the time stamps on his posts. You know whom he’s mad at today.

As a result, voters feel like they know him—like they’re in on the joke, part of the movement, personally connected to power. Many Democratic Party figures hate this. It feels to them like a debasement of the office, and, in my view, they’re right.

Although Trump’s constant communication was initially a shock to the body politic, voters developed a tolerance for it—and they have come to expect it. Whoever runs on the Democratic side in 2028 will have to be culturally omnipresent too. They shouldn’t mimic Trump’s chaos and cruelty. But they’ll have to play along with the electorate’s desire to know where they stand on everything, all the time. They’ll need a direct relationship with the voters that bypasses what’s left of media gatekeepers.

Julie, a Democrat from Arizona, said this about her party’s leaders in an April 2025 focus group: “They didn’t make people connect to them emotionally enough. And we need that emotional connection. If you look at the MAGA party, they have, albeit a bit psychotically, a very emotional connection. And we need that.” She’s recognizing that Trump built something that Democrats haven’t—a bond that goes beyond policy positions.

Looking ahead to the midterms and the 2028 presidential election, I cannot emphasize this enough: Donald Trump is not 10 feet tall, and MAGA is not invincible. Remember Arnold Schwarzenegger in Predator? “If it bleeds, we can kill it,” he said. MAGA might have all of the power right now, but it’s bleeding. Voters in the focus groups have talked about four main areas where the GOP is weakest, giving Democrats an opening.

The first is immigration. This was supposed to be Trump’s strength, and in many ways, it still is; voters consistently rate Republicans more highly on border security. But there’s a gap between what voters wanted and what Trump has delivered. Lauren, a Trump voter from Florida, captured this: “I feel like we have so many hardworking immigrants,” she said. She wants the government to “leave those people alone. Please target people entering the country now, and people—criminals—who are here now illegally. I feel like that should be our first point of action, not going into elementary schools and picking kids out of seats.”

Many of the voters who say this kind of thing aren’t open-borders liberals. They are people who wanted border security, but they believe that Trump has gone too far—that there’s a difference between strength and cruelty.

Trump is also vulnerable on the issue of corruption. Voters who expected him to fight for them are discovering that he’s been cleaning up for himself. Olan from Georgia, a 2020 Joe Biden voter and 2024 Trump voter, noted the skeeviness of Trump accepting a jet from the government of Qatar: “Everything he’s doing is basically enriching his family. I’m not saying, ‘Hey, you’re not supposed to make money,’ but I thought we’re supposed to be helping the middle class here.”

Jeffrey Epstein also remains a weak spot for Trump. “Why did he campaign on it that he’s gonna get in there and he’s gonna release the Epstein files?” Melissa, a two-time Trump voter from Pennsylvania, wondered in November. “Usually he’s super transparent, and what he says he’s gonna do, he’s gonna do.” Sam, a Gen Z Trump voter from Minnesota, said early this year, “By dragging his feet on it, it’s really like, man, some people might really just be above the law, and it’s not something that sits well with me.”

Finally, there’s the economy. What I hear from 2024 Trump voters in focus groups is simple: Trump isn’t doing the things that he told Americans he would do to fix prices. In particular, young people who voted for Trump have said that they believed him during the campaign when he promised to “build the greatest economy in the history of the world.” When he didn’t, they felt duped and let down. “There are things that are very disappointing and very rough right now,” Kim from Virginia said. “Overall, I think the job market is really hard right now,” Allison from New York said.

I know this might seem obvious to say, but the economy and cost of living remain as important as ever to voters, even while many of the long-standing rules of politics and voter behavior are shifting.

Good news for the Democrats: This is the kind of moment in which new leaders emerge. The old guard is exhausted. The appetite for change is overwhelming. People are ready—desperate, even—for something new. When I ask voters which potential candidates they’re excited about, they don’t cite boring, by-the-book, geriatric politicians. They talk about fighters who go viral.

Mike, a Massachusetts Democrat, said, “Jon Ossoff is blowing me away. He doesn’t go on and on. He’s not apologetic. He’s not defensive. He simplifies things.” Mike likes that Ossoff “just brings it down to, like, a bullet point.”

Bryan, a New York Democrat, said, “Someone like Pete Buttigieg is a fantastic communicator, articulates well, and is willing to go on as many right-wing areas and interview formats, just because he can, because he knows how to articulate and he knows how to speak to both sides.”

Leonard, another New York Democrat, praised New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “Sometimes you absolutely need a new voice, someone who actually can come in there as a renegade and not be beholden to the past, and come in there as an innovator and aim to get some things done.” Ultimately, he said, “sometimes you just need that kind of a shake-up.”

And Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s name gets brought up all the time. Adrien, a Pennsylvania Democrat, said, “She’s charismatic. She actually gives a crap about people. She knows what it’s like to be working class.” Petra, another Democrat, agreed: “She has a backbone. She’s a strong, strong woman. She’s not afraid to tell it like it is.”

Notice that this kind of appeal isn’t limited to either the party’s left wing or its center. It’s more about coming across as an authentic messenger who cares about the issues that ordinary people also care about—not the interminable moderate-versus-progressive policy discourse that animates professional political obsessives.

I know from listening to voters that they recognize a fighter when they see one. They respond to authenticity, to energy, to the sense that a leader gives a damn. And they can tell when someone is genuinely committed to changing things.

The Democratic candidates who succeed in the coming years will be the ones who articulate clearly why Trump and his movement have failed voters. They will seize on the contradictions and broken promises of the “America First” movement and build a platform that feels responsive to people’s everyday needs. They’ll center economic concerns, opportunity, the idea of rebuilding the American dream as part of a concrete plan for how people’s lives can get better.

And they’ll do it with urgency—not because they want to be like Trump but because they understand that these times demand wartime generals, not peacetime diplomats: leaders who recognize that American democracy is in a fight for its survival and are willing to act like it. The voters are ready. The question is whether the Democratic Party will listen.

This article has been adapted from Sarah Longwell’s new book, How to Eat an Elephant: One Voter at a Time.

entries.title: Misunder­standing Norman Rockwell
entries.summary: His paintings evoked an American innocence that didn’t exist—and that the nation couldn’t live up to.
entries.content:
His paintings evoked an American innocence that didn’t exist—and that the nation couldn’t live up to.

In 1976, as the country commemorated its bicentennial, an aging Norman Rockwell, then at the tail end of his career as America’s preeminent illustrator, painted his last magazine cover, Liberty Bell (Celebration). It was a tender—and notably low-key—tribute to national unity that doubled as a capstone for his body of work. For a decades-long stretch in the mid-20th century, the illustrator’s memorable images of smiling families and gentle, small-town interactions had filled the pages of national magazines, serving up a portrait of American life that was upbeat, idealistic, and reassuring. It’s a vision that has felt far away amid this year’s celebrations, once again, of the nation’s birthday.

But the Rockwellian vision of America has felt distant for a long while. That distance is why we have songs such as Lana Del Rey’s “Norman Fucking Rockwell.” It’s why the phrase like a Rockwell painting is often deployed, not simply as a descriptive but as an implicit critique of naive civic optimism. And it’s why Rockwell has served as enduring grist for artists who, although they have been influenced by his visual iconography, have at the same time been compelled to give voice to some of the more disturbing impulses that have shaped the American psyche.

No one did this more compellingly than David Lynch, the director who, over and over, turned Rockwell’s depiction of American innocence on its head. Lynch liked to recount in interviews a comment that a sound mixer on one of his films had once made to him: that his work was “like Norman Rockwell meets Hieronymus Bosch.” The filmmaker wanted to take Rockwell’s attractive but brittle surfaces, break them open, and plunge us into something deeper and darker. Understanding Lynch, in other words, is a way of understanding Rockwell. In particular, it’s a way of understanding one of the tragic effects of Rockwell’s influential vision: It’s so relentlessly benign and so morally pristine that it’s impossible to live up to. It’s an albatross slung over America’s shoulders.

Early in Lynch’s masterpiece Mulholland Drive, which turns 25 this year, is a scene that doubles as one of Lynch’s many loving homages to Rockwell. The bright-faced, wide-eyed Betty (played by Naomi Watts) has arrived in Los Angeles, where she wants to become a movie star. On the flight over, she befriended an older couple, who walk with her through the airport.

“Well, it’s time to say goodbye, Betty,” the old lady says. “It’s been so nice traveling with you.”

“Thank you, Irene. I’m so excited and nervous. It was so good to have you to talk to.”

“Remember, I’ll be watching for you on the big screen.”

“Okay, Irene. Won’t that be the day!”

They part, whereupon a look of horror cavorts across Betty’s face: Her bags are no longer at her feet!

“My bags!” she says aloud. But her panic lasts only a moment. The Rockwellian universe is briskly restored: A friendly cab driver is putting her luggage in the trunk of his taxi. “Where to?” he asks.

Only now, having toyed with us, does Lynch signal that everything we have just witnessed—the “kindness, comedy, and forgiving tristesse” that the critic Dave Hickey rightly saw as a hallmark of Rockwell’s sensibility—has been subject to a menacing undertow. Lynch returns us to the old couple, now leaving the airport inside a black limo. Strapped snugly into their seats, they’re reminiscent of overgrown children; their old heads swivel back and forth in slow motion like laughing clowns’, and their twinkling smiles suggest something just short of psychopathy.

Their grins are so unkillable, in fact, that what they most powerfully recall to me are the faces that crowd around the Thanksgiving table in one of Rockwell’s most famous images: Freedom From Want. This is one of four paintings he made from 1942 to 1943 to illustrate the “Four Freedoms” laid out by Franklin D. Roosevelt on January 6, 1941, when he provided the moral framework for America’s involvement in World War II. (The other three are Freedom of Speech, Freedom of Worship, and Freedom From Fear.) If you look closely at Freedom From Want, which is on permanent display at the Norman Rockwell Museum, in Stockbridge, Massachusetts, you see first how utterly brilliant Rockwell was.

Perhaps most striking is how monochromatic large parts of the painting are. There’s the opaque white tablecloth, a white apron, and translucent white curtains—but within all of that white is an astonishing level of variety. The round plates are glossy. The creased tablecloth is matte. A silver tureen is so shiny that it gleams white. The transparent water glasses cast silvery reflections with white highlights. And those curtains are gauzily radiant. It’s a bravura display.

Is it also somewhat stiff and sepulchral? It is! And this could kill the whole painting, except that against this almost fanatically pure still life, Rockwell—following the same principle of contrasts at the heart of Lynch’s aesthetic—sets the sparkling, animated choreography of the family. Cut off from their bodies by the picture’s vertical edges, their love-flushed heads lean in, drawn together by high spirits, humor, and the same intergenerational respect Lynch wanted us to feel between Betty and Irene in Mulholland Drive. Rockwell studied faces closely, including his own in the mirror. (That’s him smiling out of the painting’s lower right corner, like Lynch popping up as a hard-of-hearing FBI chief on Twin Peaks.) Good illustrators use facial expressions to convey action and consequence. Rockwell always sought maximum expression. Here, your gaze ping-pongs back and forth across the table, involuntarily weaving a lacy web of loving rapport.

Still, the intensity of their expressions starts to feel uncanny. The teenage boy at the far end of the table has a smile so impeccably amiable that you idly wonder whether he might ever have lost his temper. At which point the pigtailed girl next to him, who stares straight at the viewer, starts to convey something latently demonic. Next to her, you notice with a start, is a wrinkled and waxy, almost clawlike hand, which presumably belongs to the venerable paterfamilias who stands at the head of the table, but which is cut off from his body by the platter carrying the turkey.

If it’s easy to imagine the whole scene as a movie, slowed down, subtly sinister—like the scene with the grinning retirees in Mulholland Drive—that’s because Lynch’s work so effectively gives the lie to Rockwell’s.

In the good-humored and reassuringly rational world that Rockwell constructed, there was no such thing as evil. His portraits of everyday life included pratfalls, minor moral lapses, and some genuine pain, but the arc of history was always bending the right way. In its fundamental integrity, Rockwellian America was as immaculate and charismatic as that Thanksgiving table.

What is clear today is that the strain, so many decades on, of trying to make America conform to Rockwell’s softly arcadian image is too great. It’s a burden the nation cannot collectively handle and probably never could—which is why it continually demands forms of cultural release. These, over the years, have come in the form of not just Lynch’s creations but also novels such as Portnoy’s Complaint and American Psycho, and films such as Apocalypse Now. All are explosions of irrationality designed to release us from the whole Rockwellian racket and to renew our connection to darker truths.

It’s not that Lynch’s take on America was any more real than Rockwell’s. It’s that his films expressed the absurdity of trying to make actual life match the illustrator’s gorgeous yet finally intolerable image of pleasantness and perfectibility. Since Rockwell’s heyday, this image has loomed over America like an impossibly kind, wise, and accomplished parent—and like a silent rebuke.

On your way to the Norman Rockwell Museum, you may pass through the nearby town of Stockbridge, where Rockwell lived for a quarter century. He lovingly rendered its Main Street in a Christmas Eve scene painted in 1967, a year that also saw the Summer of Love, the release of Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band, and another 100,000 American troops sent to Vietnam. Fifty years ago, during the nation’s bicentennial celebrations (and two years before Rockwell died), Stockbridge staged a parade of floats with tableaux inspired by the illustrator. The procession, in which 2,000 people participated, was attended by more than 10,000. No other American artist has ever received such a tribute.

The most extraordinary room at the Rockwell museum is always the basement gallery, which is festooned with the artist’s Saturday Evening Post covers—more than 300 of them. Rockwell first walked into the offices of the mass-circulation weekly in 1916, carrying a portfolio of his artwork. His timing was excellent: This was near the beginning of a great era in illustration, when advances in printing technology transformed large-scale color illustration into an essential aspect of communication. His talent was quickly rewarded. Within four years, Rockwell had become the Post’s leading illustrator. By 1925, he was known around the nation, and before the Depression was over, he had been all but canonized—America’s leading “Painter-Patriot,” as his biographer Deborah Solomon wrote, its paragon of picture-making.

Rockwell achieved his status by painting small-town America. “I do ordinary people in everyday situations, and that’s about all I do,” he said in his 1960 memoir, My Adventures as an Illustrator. He was so successful, and so much better known than just about any other American artist, that people had great sport comparing him with his avant-garde peers in the art world. (This reputation gave rise to some amusing images: Rockwell’s The Connoisseur, from 1962, for instance, shows a portly, fastidious-looking man in a light-gray suit standing in front of a parti-color splatter painting in the manner of Jackson Pollock. When he saw The Connoisseur, Willem de Kooning, Pollock’s friend and rival, quipped that the illustrator had done it better than Pollock.)

But Rockwell never pretended to be other than he was: an artist paid to make images in service to stories. Content to be called an illustrator, he was nevertheless unsure about the difference between what he did and fine art. His confusion was legitimate. Illustration, after all, is not inherently better or worse than any other style of art. Rembrandt was, to a large extent, an illustrator, a visual artist involved in the challenge of dramatizing Biblical stories; so was Winslow Homer, and not just in his magazine work. Narrative art is difficult for the obvious reason that it’s hard to show cause and effect (the core engine of narrative) with a single image frozen in time. The illustrator’s art lies in implying both cause and effect, so that a story—with its conventional, if artificial, movement from obscured buildup to crystalline consequence—unfolds in the viewer’s mind even as the image remains static. At this, Rockwell was brilliant.

Still, professional illustrators are usually beholden to the directives of those who publish their work. In Rockwell’s case, this meant 47 years following the dictates of the Post, a magazine that sold 2 million copies a week and was avidly read by many more people. For decades, it also had an abhorrent policy (against which Rockwell chafed more and more until he finally severed ties with the magazine) of not depicting Black people except in subservient roles. After he left, Rockwell felt freer to address civil-rights-era issues, especially desegregation, which he did in such celebrated paintings as New Kids in the Neighborhood and The Problem We All Live With, his depiction, for Look magazine, of Ruby Bridges being escorted by federal marshals to her previously all-white school.

To see the Post covers gathered together is to discern a cumulative, if highly prejudicial, portrait of America spanning more than four decades. Was it a portrait that helped America understand itself? Despite its cheesiness, and notwithstanding the Post’s appalling racism, I think it did—not just because Rockwell was so good at what he did but also because he was an artist in whom humor, grace, and loving appreciation easily commingled. These attributes were tethered, moreover, to a larger civic-mindedness. His best paintings are not only ingeniously constructed and brilliantly colored—they’re also richly humane. Stories are connected to our curiosity about how the world works, and for Rockwell, this curiosity was rooted in everyday life.

“The commonplaces of America are to me the richest subjects in art,” he wrote in 1936. “Boys batting flies on vacant lots; little girls playing jacks on the front steps; old men plodding home at twilight, umbrellas in hand—all of these things arouse feeling in me. Commonplaces never become tiresome. It is we who become tired when we cease to become curious and appreciative.”

Rockwell’s portrait of life in America is certainly kitsch. (Kitsch, Milan Kundera wrote, is “the absolute denial of shit, in both the literal and figurative sense of the word”; it “excludes everything from its purview which is essentially unacceptable in human existence.”) Still, his vision has had an enduring afterlife. Inevitably, its narrative potency—in particular its appeal to nostalgia—has been exploited across the political sphere.

A Forbes columnist writing in 2012, more than three decades after the illustrator’s death, described the GOP primaries that year as “a process by which the candidate who demonstrates the most willingness to bring back Norman Rockwell’s America wins.” In 2020, shortly after he was elected, President Biden posted on Instagram a Hollywood ad agency’s reimagining of Rockwell’s United Nations mosaic, The Golden Rule, populated (in both the original and the adaptation) by a diverse group of Americans. And last year, President Trump’s Department of Homeland Security posted—without permission, prompting uproar—several of Rockwell’s paintings (including Salute the Flag and Working On the Statue of Liberty) to its social-media account.

But it is not just this country’s politicians who are in Rockwell’s thrall. The painter’s affable pictorial rhetoric has cast a spell over holiday celebrations, modes of patriotic display, civic relations, even family relations. He was such a powerful image-maker that he created prototypes—ideals, really—of how life ought to be. And his work leaves a lingering sense that, if you want to be a happy American, you must (consciously or otherwise) reenact Rockwellian rituals.

What Rockwell visualized was, of course, suffocatingly narrow. The critic Robert Hughes once called it “a dream world of small-town America.” In this America, Hughes wrote, “kids did not snort angel dust and get one another pregnant; they stole apples and swam in forbidden water holes but said grace before meals. All soldiers were nice boys from next door; all politicians were benevolent or harmlessly bumbling.”

Big cities were subject to the roiling forces of unchecked capitalism and the blights of anonymity, rootlessness, and exploitation. Small towns, in Rockwell’s view, provided antidotes to all this. (He died well before the peak of deindustrialization and the first wave of the opioid epidemic.) They offered daily connection, neighborly interdependence, and, always, the lubricant of good humor (qualities that oiled Lynch’s twisted soap opera, Twin Peaks, too).

To say that Rockwell’s America never existed is not to say that Rockwellian virtues do not exist; they do, all around us, every day. It’s only to acknowledge that the starched-white fiction these virtues cumulatively illustrate is by now so stained and sullied that just trying to keep up the pretense can trigger a kind of collective hysteria.

The psychic pressure of trying to live up to an impossible ideal deeply interested Lynch. It produced his bifurcated visions of Rockwellian naivete and raw malevolence. In Rockwell, a diner is a place where a policeman can buy a runaway boy a milkshake before taking him home to his parents. In Lynch’s Mulholland Drive, Winkie’s Diner is where a tormenting nightmare becomes atrociously real.

The night after I returned from Stockbridge, I rewatched Lynch’s Wild at Heart, his bizarre, hilarious, and very disturbing spin on Bonnie and Clyde. A lot of the action takes place in Big Tuna, a kind of anti-Stockbridge in the Texas badlands where evil thrives. The rusty, fish-shaped sign on the edge of town has been defaced with an expletive.

The film’s main characters, Sailor and Lula (Nicholas Cage and Laura Dern), are deliberately cartoonlike, avatars of innocence transplanted to a context so malignant that it eats away at their mutual infatuation. When Lula picks up Sailor from prison, she brings him his favorite snakeskin jacket. “Did I ever tell you that this here jacket represents a symbol of my individuality and my belief in personal freedom?” he declares, like a third-grader reciting the Pledge of Allegiance.

“About 50,000 times!” answers Lula, with no hint of a rebuke, only adoration. But that Rockwellian earnestness is no match for a setting corrupted by a hit man, a depraved mother, and the sniggering malevolence of Willem Dafoe. When Sailor confesses to having once worked for the man who murdered her father, Lula becomes pensive: “It’s just shocking,” she says, “when things aren’t the way you thought they were.”

Rockwell expressed a similar sentiment before he died. It had been his idea to paint the Four Freedoms. He first took the proposal to the United States Office of War Information, where it was rejected, but after the paintings were published in the Post and received a huge response (60,000 letters were sent in by readers), the OWI reversed course and printed 2.5 million posters of the paintings, which the agency used to sell war bonds.

In 1977, near the end of his life, Rockwell said: “I really believed that the war against Hitler would bring the Four Freedoms to everyone. But I couldn’t paint that today. I just don’t believe it. I was doing this best-possible-world, Santa-down-the-chimney, lovely-kids-adoring-their-kindly-grandpa sort of thing. And I liked it, but now I’m sick of it.”

Lynch saw and loved Rockwell’s America—really loved it, as a child loves their parents—but something compelled him to break its surface and turn it violently inside out. This was a psychic and an artistic reaction, which is very different from a civic or political one. Maybe what America has to do with Norman Rockwell, as all children must eventually do with their parents, is figure out how to love him and leave him at the same time.

entries.title: A War of Assassinations
entries.summary: The U.S. and Iran are engaged in a conflict that is massive in scale but personal in nature.
entries.content:
The U.S. and Iran are engaged in a conflict that is massive in scale but personal in nature.

Sign up for our newsletter about national security here.

The latest Iranian assassination threat arrived last month as a video called “Where to Kill Barron Trump,” promising $10 million for the murder of the U.S. president’s youngest child. Less than 24 hours later, on social media, the State Department re-upped its own $10 million bounty for “information” about five leaders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, including Majid Khademi, the intelligence-office commander.

The State Department offer, part of its Rewards for Justice program, first circulated on March 20. A few weeks later, the Israeli government took credit for killing Khademi in an air strike on Tehran, adding an ominous note to the U.S. government’s decision to recirculate the poster. I asked the State Department whether this was deliberate, so soon after Iran’s announcement of a $10 million bounty for the president’s son. An official declined to comment on “internal deliberations” but noted that information obtained through the Rewards for Justice program can be used to “support a range of U.S. government responses to disrupt threats, consistent with U.S. law and policy.”

Threats of assassination have, from the start, been dark and disruptive subplots of the U.S.-Iran war. Both sides have made the tactic central to their national strategies, though the executions have been rather one-sided, as President Trump and his Israeli allies have overseen the widespread killing of Iran’s senior leadership. The impact on the American government has nonetheless been profound. “We are aware of ongoing threats from the Iranian regime and its proxies and take them extremely seriously,” the State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told me in a written statement. “We will not hesitate to act to protect U.S. government officials, current and former, and their families.”

Iran clearly sees the propaganda value of threatening American officials. Murals in Tehran now depict Trump, members of his family, and other senior U.S. officials in coffins. Hey Terrorist! Get Ready To Die, reads one apparently AI-generated billboard that shows Trump looking skyward on a golf course. Iran’s army chief promised a $30,000 bounty last month to any Iranian man who kills or captures a U.S. service member, without specifying a target location. (Women would be paid twice as much.) In addition to threatening Barron, Iranian outlets have released a “How to Kill Melania” video about the first lady, and published a target list of multiple world leaders and U.S. Cabinet members. “The criminal, disgraceful murderers of the martyred Leader, whose names are fully documented from the highest to the lowest ranks, will carry their dream of a peaceful death in bed to the grave,” Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, the nation’s supreme leader, said in a written statement on July 11. He succeeded his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was assassinated by Israeli air strikes on his compound on the first day of the war.

But the Iranian campaign is not limited to posturing. Last month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced that “Iran tried to murder” one of his sons, an apparent reference to 35-year-old Yair Netanyahu. In July, Israeli intelligence described an Iranian plot to use a French resident, Servet Ozkur, to recruit assassins to target senior officials in Israel. Iran has repeatedly sent assassins to kill Trump and other U.S. officials, according to the Justice Department, as punishment for Trump’s 2020 order to assassinate the Iranian military commander Qassem Soleimani. About a week after the start of the Iran war this year, a federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Asif Merchant, the architect of one of two alleged Iranian plots in the United States. Prosecutors claimed that Merchant, a Pakistani national trained by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, had entered the United States with orders to recruit “mafia” hit men. But Merchant ended up speaking with undercover officers, telling them they would receive instructions on the target after he left the country. He was arrested before he made it to the airport and faces a sentence of up to life in prison.

Assassination was clearly on Trump’s mind when the elder Khamenei was killed. “I got him before he got me,” Trump told ABC News’s Jonathan Karl in March. “They tried twice. Well, I got him first.”

The U.S. presidency has long been a dangerous job. Trump has faced at least three assassination attempts by domestic assailants. Those attacks, along with Iran’s threats, are reshaping the lives of the president and his advisers, and restricting Trump’s ability to interact with the country he governs.

Earlier this year, at a summit in Ankara, Trump told reporters that his own chance of dying in office was 5.2 percent, dramatically higher than that of race-car drivers and bull riders. (He did not provide a source for his comparisons. Of the 45 men elected president, four, or about 8.9 percent, have been assassinated in office.) Trump said at the same appearance that “I’m No. 1 on the kill list for Iran.” Then the president turned his traveling press corps and two Cabinet officials into flying decoys when he snuck out a side door of Air Force One as it sat on the tarmac, to avoid a purported Iranian plot to target the plane. After a short ride in a catering truck, he boarded a different plane and flew to his next stop, in England.

The logistics of presidential travel are now far more burdensome than they were when Trump first took office. The Secret Service’s personal-protection budget has nearly doubled since 2016. New airspace restrictions have been imposed over Mar-a-Lago. Lafayette Park, just north of the White House, has been closed for months for security; there are plans to install new fencing that would further obstruct public access. The new White House ballroom, the U.S. Army has argued in court, is “essential to ensure uninterrupted command and control” given the new threats of a drone attack.

A number of Cabinet officials and top White House aides now live on military bases to protect themselves and their families, in certain cases because of specific foreign threats. Other rank-and-file White House advisers, unnerved by a homegrown assassination attempt at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner in April, have receded from the city where they live. “People are just more careful about where they go and, frankly, how often they are out in public,” a White House official told me.

All of this portends a grim future in which assassination moves from an extreme risk to a more commonplace threat. Perhaps that will lead to a reassessment of its use as both a tool of U.S. foreign policy and a way to menace an enemy’s senior officials. “At some stage, I do wonder whether politicians thinking about themselves actually come to the conclusion that they are signing their own death warrants or essentially undermining their own democracies” by promoting the extrajudicial killing of their enemies, Simon Ball, a professor at the University of Leeds, in England, and the author of Death to Order: A Modern History of Assassination, told me. He added that assassination threats are now such a regular fact of life that to have protection against them confers a macabre prestige. “Elite status is defined by whether you have protection from assassination,” Ball said. “If you do not have protection, you are not important. You are little people.”

The assassination threats from Iran have had a big impact on Trump’s life, but administration officials contend that the threats have played no role in Trump’s decision to attack Iran, which he did in June 2025 and again in February, citing the need to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, among other reasons. “He has never equated their threats against him as a reason for doing this,” one senior administration official told me. “He views the threats against him as a part of the job.”

But the military has made killing those who allegedly threaten the president part of the campaign. Four days after the conflict began, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth walked into the Pentagon with triumphant news about an Israeli strike the night before. The U.S. and Israel, he announced, had hunted down the “leader of the unit who attempted to assassinate President Trump.”

On the one hand, Hegseth suggested that the strike was a personal victory for the president. “Iran tried to kill President Trump, and President Trump got the last laugh,” Hegseth told reporters. On the other hand, he said that Trump had not concerned himself with the strikes. Going after the president’s assassins, Hegseth said, “was not the focus of the effort by any stretch of the imagination, in fact, never raised by the president or anybody else.” Instead, by his account, it seems to have just sort of happened as a favor to the boss. “I ensured, and others ensured, that those who were responsible for that were eventually part of the target list,” Hegseth said.

Trump has similarly blurred these lines, sometimes focusing on the threat and at other times dismissing it. After Cole Tomas Allen, a tutor from California, was apprehended while attempting to infiltrate the Correspondents’ Dinner armed with multiple guns and knives, Trump told reporters that “I don’t think about” the prospect of assassination, and “if I did, I wouldn’t be doing a very good job here.” But hours before B-2 bombers struck Iran in June last year, the president told reporters after disembarking Air Force One in New Jersey that they had put themselves in danger just by standing next to him. “Be careful,” he said.

Trump has also made clear that any nation that assassinated him would face apocalyptic retaliation. “I’ve left instructions. If they do it, they get obliterated. There won’t be anything left,” he said of Iran two weeks after taking office last year. This July, hours before Mojtaba promised revenge for his father’s death, Trump posted on social media that even an attempted assassination on him would result in a military response: “Orders have already been given, and the U.S. Military is ready, willing, and able, for a one year period of time, subject to extension, to completely decimate and destroy all areas of Iran.”

Iranian officials have been ambiguous about how seriously the U.S. should take its threats. Days after the Barron video began circulating on Tebyan.net, an arm of the Iranian government’s propaganda machine, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, called the threats against Barron a lie and dismissed the alleged plot against Trump in Turkey as “false news.” But in the same interview with Lebanon’s Al-Manar TV, Rezaei—whose predecessor was killed by Israeli strikes in March—said Iran would send Netanyahu “to hell.”

The claim received scant coverage. World leaders plotting to kill one another has become routine.

entries.title: The Prodigy Problem
entries.summary: Leopold Aschenbrenner claimed to know the future of AI. His investors lost billions.
entries.content:
Leopold Aschenbrenner claimed to know the future of AI. His investors lost billions.

In the fall of 2007, as the American housing market began to buckle, a Morgan Stanley bond trader named Howie Hubler lost $9 billion. The bellicose former linebacker believed that he had structured his subprime-mortgage deals in a way that would outsmart the market. Instead, Hubler’s folly amounted to the largest trading loss in history.

Until this summer, that is, when Leopold Aschenbrenner managed to lose nearly four times as much. At age 24.

The implosion of Aschenbrenner’s AI hedge fund, Situational Awareness, over the course of a few days in late July was by any standard remarkable, and not just for the enormous sums involved. Aschenbrenner was the valedictorian of his Columbia University class at age 19. He worked for OpenAI before being fired amid murky circumstances, at which point he published a viral 165-page essay (also called “Situational Awareness”) that predicted the arrival of artificial general intelligence—an AI so advanced that it would meet or exceed all human capabilities—by 2027.

“I probably either personally know or am one degree of separation from everyone who could plausibly run The Project,” he wrote. He founded his hedge fund on that promise of access and soon turned a $225 million initial investment into $45 billion, before he was forced to unload the majority of his positions—$35 billion, the value of United Airlines—in a fire sale the same week that he was set to be married. The Securities and Exchange Commission is now investigating the collapse, though Aschenbrenner has not been accused of any wrongdoing. (He did not respond to a request for comment.)

Aschenbrenner had been considered the “Nostradamus of AI,” a clairvoyant who saw what was coming for the world. His spectacular failure reveals how eager Silicon Valley is to invest its billions in the dubious hands of a kid who confidently proclaims what he doesn’t actually know. Just as Hubler’s loss presaged the Great Recession, Aschenbrenner’s story of hubris may foreshadow a larger risk for today’s AI-driven boom, if it continues to stake its future on the bluster of young savants.

“There’s this hunger for insight porn in Silicon Valley,” Amjad Masad, the founder and CEO of the popular AI-coding platform Replit, told me. “If you’re able to write something really good that creates this dopamine rush in people—like, Oh, I just saw the future—then you’re going to be able to attract a lot of capital and money and potentially talent.”

This was the appeal of Leopold Aschenbrenner.

Born in Berlin to a pair of doctors, Aschenbrenner has said that Germany lacked “the appreciation of excellence” that would have allowed him to thrive; America beckoned, and at 15, he headed to Columbia. One of his first gigs after college was for the FTX Future Fund—the philanthropic arm of the crypto exchange run by Sam Bankman-Fried, the effective-altruism adherent who was later convicted of fraud. This brought Aschenbrenner into a circle that was quirky even by Silicon Valley standards.

Aschenbrenner lived at Bankman-Fried’s compound in the Bahamas—right up until he resigned, along with the rest of the FTX Future Fund staff members, as the crypto exchange came tumbling down. Soon after, he took up with the effective-altruism crowd in San Francisco. One of his close associates told me about attending “Iliad wrestling parties,” where people would drink wine, read passages from The Iliad, strip naked, and grapple with one another. Aschenbrenner liked to describe, with full sincerity, his goal of owning a galaxy, The Wall Street Journal reported. His now-wife worked for Bankman-Fried too and is currently chief of staff to Anthropic’s CEO. Their wedding plans included panel discussions and colloquia.

The more unusual Aschenbrenner seemed, the more this played in his favor. His essay, which set the wonkiest corners of Silicon Valley ablaze in 2024, laid out a mission to bet on superintelligence “before the decade is out.” His premise was simple: “You can see the future first in San Francisco,” Aschenbrenner wrote. “Let me tell you what we see.”

Aschenbrenner’s predictions were illustrated by charts and graphs and all manner of calculations, but really, they were carried along by his rhetoric. “I can see it,” Aschenbrenner wrote. “I can see how AGI will be built.” Both outsiders and insiders in Silicon Valley “are really confused about what’s going on and therefore are drawn to people who seem to have a really confident, clear picture of the future,” Helen Toner, an AI expert who sat on the board of OpenAI, told me. Those who would presume to doubt Aschenbrenner’s judgment merely lacked the extra-special access that made his vision so clear. And central to this access was a fervent ideological commitment to the idea of superintelligence.

Aschenbrenner and his cohort proudly describe themselves as “AGI-pilled.” That is, they believe AGI to be around the corner and its benefits to be self-evident. They extoll the ability of a superintelligent machine to heal the world of its ills, thereby serving the effective-altruism philosophy many of them share.

Christopher Manning, an early AI pioneer whose research laid the groundwork for large language models, told me that Silicon Valley has a “propensity to naively believe in gurus.” Aschenbrenner played the role to perfection, projecting an unshakable conviction in himself and his theory of the case. By this summer, Aschenbrenner controlled more money than the Wall Street investor Bill Ackman manages in his famed Pershing Square Capital, a level of funding that Manning, himself an investor in AI companies, called “manifestly crazy.”

Even as Aschenbrenner’s assets grew, his team remained tiny. Situational Awareness was, essentially, Aschenbrenner. This approach seemed to be validated by the most important metric of all: his returns, which were, for someone in his position, probably without precedent. In just two years, Aschenbrenner was up more than 1,000 percent. His core insight was understanding the second- and third-order effects of AGI—he bet on the chip manufacturers, data centers, and energy infrastructure required for the rapid expansion he predicted. Yet it turned out that Situational Awareness had achieved its rapid success by making extraordinary, over-leveraged trades, sometimes borrowing $3 or $4 for every $1 of capital it invested. When Aschenbrenner’s bets took a momentary pummeling this summer and banks came asking for their money back, the fixation on the impending arrival of AGI no longer seemed quite so wise: The hedge fund had failed to hedge.

Around the time that Hubler’s trades collapsed in 2007, John Arnold, a cerebral Texan hedge-fund manager, was the boy genius of the markets, having become the youngest billionaire in America.
