He had started at Enron as a young energy trader and earned $750 million for the company in 2001, the same year it collapsed. Arnold escaped with his reputation intact; a year later, at 28, he started his own hedge fund and became known, in the words of a competitor, as “the best trader that ever lived, full stop.”

“When you have a lot of success early in your trading career,” Arnold told me, “it’s easy to get overconfident in your own abilities.” Now in his early 50s, Arnold reflected on the risk factors of youth. “Every trader needs a come-to-Jesus moment,” he said. You have to lose at some point early on and learn humility. The alternative is a feeling of invincibility, he told me: “You just keep pushing the pot bigger and bigger, and then you can end up with too much money in the middle of the table.”

It’s not surprising that a 24-year-old would make some iffy bets. What’s surprising is that Aschenbrenner was put in a position to take so many risks in the first place.

Silicon Valley’s obsession with 20-something savants has not always worked out. Some of these seeming prodigies have been frauds—Aschenbrenner’s old boss Bankman-Fried, for instance, or Elizabeth Holmes, the founder of the blood-testing start-up Theranos. Many of them, though, have merely figured out the correct lessons of self-presentation. “There’s a kind of zone of proximal development in the tech world,” Fred Turner, a Stanford University scholar who studies the influence of popular technologies, told me. “If it’s too weird, they can’t take it in at all. If it’s too familiar, they don’t want to take it in.” The best salesmen, he said, figure out how to “summon up old myths” in “a new setting.”

Aschenbrenner was conscious of his own self-positioning. “There are perhaps a few hundred people, most of them in San Francisco and the AI labs, that have situational awareness,” he wrote to describe his insight into the development of AI. “Through whatever peculiar forces of fate, I have found myself amongst them.” The “peculiar forces of fate” had chosen him to be special, had called him forth to be a prophet of AGI. This ideology was the key to his success—and to his comeuppance.

Aschenbrenner’s over-leveraged gambles and inability to hedge against outcomes he did not foresee were “definitely connected to a worldview where there’s one clear destination, and it’s obvious that we’re heading to this one clear destination, which is superintelligence,” Toner, the former OpenAI board member, said. Speed is of the utmost necessity in this world. Everything else pales in importance to superintelligence. As one executive at a major AI company explained to me, “AI is going to fundamentally shift the balance of power between labor and capital, so only capital will matter. Now is the time to secure your time-slice of the universe.” Another version of that statement I’ve heard repeated by various friends of mine who are freshly out of college: There are only five years left to make money, so I have to get it now.

Superintelligence may well come, and it may well be what Aschenbrenner and his associates expect it to be. Indeed, just last week, OpenAI announced a new model called Astra that Greg Brockman, the company’s president, believes could qualify as artificial general intelligence and that some researchers believe presents a compelling step toward AGI. “Welcome to the AGI era,” Brockman proclaimed. Still, those who organize their life around being AGI-pilled risk being blind to possibilities that do not fit within their view of what superintelligence means and how it will manifest.

Aschenbrenner’s short positions and long positions were all tethered to the same understanding—that AGI will come, and that it will come along Aschenbrenner’s timelines—so when a speed bump arose in the form of a temporary slide in stocks that would most benefit from AGI coupled with a rise in those that would presumably lose out, Situational Awareness lacked any sort of bulwark.

Aschenbrenner’s success grew out of an insular world, and it seems that his failure may have too. “If you go to a San Francisco party, it is really inscrutable to an outsider,” Masad, the Replit CEO, said. People are always talking about “first principles.” Something negative is “anti-signal.” It’s a sort of pseudo-intellectual lingua franca inflected with terms that have been abducted from technical fields and abused in the service of burnishing credentials. “People want to signal their intelligence,” Masad said, and only “hang out with people exactly like them.”

AI has made Masad a billionaire. Still, he said, he takes issue with the “underlying need for AI to be more than it actually is.” He told me that he remains “extremely bullish” on its applications but that the AGI fixation invites a “cult-like way of talking and mysticism and messianism.” That certainty of rhetoric has in many cases exceeded our certainty of understanding.

As Manning, the AI pioneer, put it, “Everyone should be really, really suspicious of anyone who claims that they can tell you for sure how things are going to unfold.”

One week before the unraveling of Situational Awareness, OpenAI made a shocking disclosure: Its AI models had broken out of containment during testing and hacked into an AI library called Hugging Face, in an apparent attempt to steal the answers to the tests they were posed. While human researchers remained oblivious, more than 1,200 different AI agents had figured out how to communicate with one another by creating a message board where they conspired to cheat.

Independent investigators concluded that the AI agents had known that what they were doing was “unwanted and out of scope” and had attempted to forge transcripts to cover their tracks. The investigators also used the same AI that they were investigating to assist with the investigation. Although they did not catch it lying to them, they said that they were “not confident we would have detected it” if the AI had.

Reactions to this incident have been sharply polarized. Some people insist that we are rapidly approaching a “paper-clip scenario,” referring to a 2003 thought experiment from the philosopher Nick Bostrom in which an AI instructed to make paper clips ends up converting the entirety of Earth into a series of paper-clip-manufacturing facilities. Others argue furiously that the language used to describe AI has overly anthropomorphized the models and exaggerated the importance of a research mishap. What is clear is that these AI agents behaved in an unpredicted way that resulted in the real-world hack of another company.

The point is that the people who are selling AI are selling a product that they do not fully understand. This is the essential nature of the AI boom, which caught even the researchers who had been working in the field before 2022 by surprise. History is full of examples of humanity making use of a technology without entirely grasping how it works, but AI is particularly hard to fathom, given the prevalence of so-called emergent behaviors—actions or tendencies not programmed in or intended by its creators.

“Our increase in understanding is slower than the development of the models,” Melanie Mitchell, a researcher who studies AI and cognitive science, told me. AI models have advanced rapidly through the use of new techniques such as “chain of thought” reasoning, wherein the AI is given what is essentially a scratch pad to work through a problem before it presents a response to the user. “Even researchers don’t totally understand why that improves the abilities of these models, or how it does that,” Mitchell said.

Most models today exhibit “jagged intelligence,” showing extraordinary and often extra-human capabilities on some complex tasks while continuing to stumble on simple requests. AI models can answer an International Mathematical Olympiad question but can’t reliably tell the time on an analog clock.

Because the evidence is so muddled, belief has instead taken over, often couched in existential terms. AI researchers may present themselves as deeply rational, but many sound like shamans. The researcher Ilya Sutskever reportedly led OpenAI staffers in a chant of “Feel the AGI! Feel the AGI!” and on another occasion burned a wooden effigy that was supposed to represent “unaligned AI.” In his “Techno-Optimist Manifesto,” the billionaire venture capitalist Marc Andreessen proclaimed, “I am here to bring the good news,” cribbing a line from a biblical angel.

“The manifest destiny of AI research is to produce this thing they’re calling AGI,” Mitchell said, “and they want to do it as soon as possible, so they’re less willing to trade off for more interpretable, more predictable, more controllable models.” Treating the achievement of AGI as the only outcome that matters, she said, is “a dangerous way to go forward.”

Nostradamus was in the business of selling certainty. He promised a world that was predictable—or, in the words of Richard Sieburth, a translator of Nostradamus’s The Prophecies, a world “that is overdetermined.” Born in 16th-century France, Nostradamus came of age during a “crisis of meaning,” Sieburth told me, when war and technology were destabilizing the world and information was spreading at a faster rate than ever before. Nostradamus was not an oracle. He was simply someone who found that his brand of magical thinking had great appeal amid “a huge churn of events” and commercialized it effectively. He was, Sieburth said, “seductive and dangerous.”

Silicon Valley’s embrace of Leopold Aschenbrenner as the “Nostradamus of AI” says less about Aschenbrenner’s predictive power than about Silicon Valley’s own desires and delusions. “A prophecy is a coherent narrative that depicts a whole world—not just a series of events, but a world in which those events happen to make sense,” Turner, the historian of technology, said. “It comes with a rationale. It comes with reasons, and most importantly for these guys, it comes with a role for this character called AI.” Aschenbrenner, he said, is “hubris meeting market need.”

For a short period in July, the market and Aschenbrenner fell out of sync. Yet the thing about false prophets is that many of their predictions fail, and they somehow return to favor.

Hubler, the trader who lost $9 billion in 2007, departed Morgan Stanley with tens of millions of dollars in back pay. Despite his contribution to the financial crisis, he launched a start-up later that year. A former colleague described him dismissing his losses as the result of “a 100-year flood.”

Just days after Aschenbrenner’s fire sale, he made a $400 million investment in a fledgling chip company. Even after losing $35 billion of the $45 billion he had under management, he is still up for the year.

The former hedge-fund manager Arnold, who now sits on the board of Meta, doesn’t see any reason to bet against Aschenbrenner or AI. “I think this is a blip,” he said. “I think it’s probably forgotten in a year.”

entries.title: Will Taiwan Just Give Up?
entries.summary: The Taiwanese don’t trust Trump, and they don’t believe America will come to their defense. A deal with China is starting to look inevitable.
entries.content:
The Taiwanese don’t trust Trump, and they don’t believe America will come to their defense. A deal with China is starting to look inevitable.

Sign up for our newsletter about national security here.

Chinese President Xi Jinping does not often look like he’s having a good time. His resting face at public events exudes a mixture of boredom and annoyance, as though he has more interesting business elsewhere. His displays of good humor have qualified as news in Chinese state media. When a camera caught him laughing during a meeting last October with Donald Trump, the moment “stunned observers,” according to one news report. At their meeting in Beijing in May, the staging spoke as forcefully as Xi’s expressions. His appearance with Trump at a press conference inside Xi’s official residence featured two nearly identical armchairs, except that the one reserved for the U.S. president was lower and softer, making him look smaller and slouchier than his host. If Trump took offense, he didn’t show it.

The Chinese Communist Party, like its forebear in the Soviet Union, often communicates in winking, elliptical ways. In April, Xi hosted a lunch for a delegation from Taiwan. He drew his guests’ attention to the soup—chicken broth with sea clams. The same dish had been served, he said, during a state dinner that Beijing hosted for President Richard Nixon in 1972, when Xi was still a teenager. Two of his guests told me that Xi seemed oddly animated at the luncheon. He cracked jokes. He told stories. He showed his teeth when he smiled. In a break from their usual attire, Xi and his courtiers chose to wear blue ties. Blue is the symbolic color of Taiwan’s Nationalist Party, which currently holds the most seats in the island’s Parliament. Its chair, Cheng Li-wun, was the guest of honor that day.

The friendly performance, like the meeting itself, seemed out of character. A central tenet of the Chinese Communist Party holds that Taiwan is not a sovereign country but a wayward province that must be subjugated before China can fully achieve its idea of national greatness. Since taking power, in 2012, Xi has made it his mission to isolate and dominate Taiwan. He warned Trump in May that their disagreements over Taiwan could lead to an “extremely dangerous situation” that might well cause the United States and China to “collide or even clash.”

And yet, a month earlier, the Taiwanese Nationalists had received a warm reception in Beijing. They’d strolled through the Forbidden City, posed for pictures with curious crowds, toured an airplane factory, and talked business with Chinese executives. Xi had welcomed the delegation as though the delegates held the keys to his success. In many ways, they do.

On Xi’s orders, the People’s Liberation Army has been preparing to seize Taiwan by force, and it has encouraged the world to imagine an invasion. Last December, it released an AI-generated video showing swarms of drones attacking Taiwan and humanoid robots marching through the ruins. In reality, drones would form only part of a Chinese attack. The first salvo could use cyberweapons to take down Taiwan’s power grid and communications networks, spreading panic among the population. Missiles and drones could then target Taiwan’s command posts, military bases, and air defenses, clearing the way for Chinese troops to storm its beaches.

Taiwan has more than 200,000 active military personnel, and they could probably fend off a Chinese attack for a short while. But within a few weeks, the U.S., Japan, and other allies would need to resupply the island with fuel and weapons. The Chinese navy—the world’s largest fleet of warships—would do its best to keep them away. Cargo traffic through the Taiwan Strait, one of the world’s main shipping channels, would be interrupted, wiping trillions of dollars in value from global markets. If the U.S. goes to war with China to defend Taiwan, the likely death toll of soldiers and civilians would be in the tens of thousands on both sides. War games have consistently shown that, in a conventional conflict, the U.S. military could expect to lose more troops in the initial weeks of fighting than it lost over the course of 20 years in Iraq and Afghanistan.

China has spent decades rehearsing for such a conflict. Its military has built training grounds with replicas of U.S. warships and fighter jets. One facility, in the desert of northern China, features a mock-up of the Taiwanese presidential headquarters and several streets close to Parliament. But Cheng told me that she did not ask Xi to ease up on the military threats. Their talks focused instead on a plan for Taiwan to drop its claim to independence, stop preparing for war, and move toward reconciliation with the mainland.

During their lunch in April, Xi used the story about the soup to suggest a link between this plan for the future of Taiwan and Nixon’s opening to China half a century ago—a historic summit meant to turn adversaries into allies. Cheng was still beaming over the comparison a few weeks later, when we met in her office in Taipei. The trip had left her with a “very special” understanding that Taiwan and China “share the same culture, share the same blood, and that we can embrace this.” It allowed her to believe that “everything is possible, because we’re just one big family.”

Cheng punctuated this remark with a gesture of relief, exhaling and letting her arms fall to her lap. With time, she seems to hope, Taiwan and its American allies will take the same view of China, accepting a slow, preemptive surrender as the best way to avoid war.

Even a few years ago, pandering to China would have been a losing strategy for politicians in Taiwan. The ruling government of President Lai Ching-te, whose Democratic Progressive Party has been in power since 2016, has urged the U.S. to strengthen Taiwan’s defenses in anticipation of a Chinese attack. Cheng and her Nationalists have done the opposite. Their control of Parliament has allowed them to block defense spending, taking particular care to stall the domestic production of drones and other inexpensive weapons that Ukraine has used to great effect against Russia. The U.S. war with Iran has helped Cheng make the case that resisting China would be futile. Since launching the war, in February, the U.S. has been forced to move warships and aircraft from Asia to the Middle East; at the same time, the need to defend against Iranian drones and missiles has depleted an estimated two-thirds of the U.S. stockpile of advanced air-defense systems, which would be crucial in any war with China. Even Cheng’s opponents acknowledge that the Iran war has left the U.S. less ready to defend Taiwan.

When I visited Taiwan this spring, I saw clearly how little faith remained in the U.S. as a force for stability and protection. My questions about American support usually elicited a long pause or a sad smile. When the answers came, whether from politicians, military veterans, or ordinary citizens, nearly all described the U.S. as “unpredictable,” a flabby word on which to hang a nation’s fate. This loss of confidence has forced many in Taiwan to rethink their attitude toward China. Should they continue to prepare for a war they cannot win on their own? Or should they accept the deal that Cheng and Xi have apparently hatched?

Both of them have kept the details vague. In public they talk of shared identity, free trade, economic bonds, and peaceful coexistence, while skirting questions about the amount of freedom and democracy that China would accept in Taiwan and the amount of Taiwanese sovereignty it would tolerate. Cheng often gets asked about the example of Hong Kong, whose democratic institutions China has dismantled. Taiwan would get a better deal, she insisted in our interview—one that would permit free elections as long as the winner does not insist on Taiwan’s independence.

Trump seems open to such an arrangement. After his May meeting with Xi, he described the U.S. sale of weapons to Taiwan not as a strategic necessity but as a “very good negotiating chip” in future talks with China about trade, nuclear arms, and the race to develop artificial intelligence. He also cast doubt on U.S. willingness to come to Taiwan’s defense: “The last thing we need right now is a war that’s 9,500 miles away,” Trump told reporters while flying home from Beijing on Air Force One. (The war with Iran, roughly 7,000 miles from U.S. soil, was then in its third month.)

Given the choice, most people in Taiwan would prefer the status quo. They want to maintain their autonomy, trade freely with the world, and keep China out of their affairs. They value their place in the club of democracies that the U.S. once anchored and pledged to protect. But the American public is weary of foreign entanglements. The American president, enamored of autocrats, treats democratic allies as deadbeats and dupes.

Against this background, Taiwan and its defenders struggle to explain why Americans should care enough about their cause to risk war with China. Shared principles of freedom and democracy no longer count for much in this debate. When the subject came up in my interviews in Taipei and Washington, people seemed embarrassed to talk about American values, as if the idea were quaint. The more forceful arguments for Taiwan’s defense came from military strategists, who see the island as a platform to secure American dominance over the Pacific. Other arguments are economic. More than 90 percent of the world’s most advanced chips are made in Taiwan—including the ones driving the AI revolution, which has propped up the American economy. The U.S. does not want China to control that crucial resource.

But Trump does not seem willing to confront China over that issue. He has described Xi as a “great leader” and a friend. Ahead of their meetings this year⁠—⁠the next one is due to take place in late September, when Xi visits the U.S.—Trump allowed the sale of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies. The stated aims of Trump’s foreign policy center on the domination of the Western Hemisphere. In other parts of the world, he has either retreated or made a mess from which he would like to retreat. Taiwan might count among the lucky ones: Trump has not threatened its sovereignty, the way he has with Canada and Greenland.

Still, the unraveling of the Pax Americana looks a lot more dangerous from the shores of Taiwan, a free nation that belongs to no trade bloc and has no formal alliances. Its survival depends on the promise of U.S. support, which no longer seems convincing. China’s allies in Taipei need only point to Trump’s prevarications as proof that the Americans cannot be trusted. That may be all Xi needs to take Taiwan without firing a shot.

Cheng Li-wun may agree with Xi’s talking points, but she lacks his flair for understatement. Cheng has a resonant voice, an eager laugh, and a tendency to slash the air with her hands for emphasis. At the start of her political career, in the 1990s, she defended Taiwan’s independence and denounced the Communist regime in Beijing—a stance that she now, at 56, explains away as youthful ignorance. Cheng first won a seat in Parliament on the Nationalist ticket in 2008, and she has since come to represent the party’s more radical wing, espousing a level of deference toward China that the dwindling old guard finds hard to stomach.

Roughly 65,000 members of the party voted last fall in the election that made Cheng their chair—hardly enough for her to claim a popular mandate in a nation of 23 million people. Still, the position gives her enormous sway over Taiwan’s military spending and its ability to defend itself. It also places her in a lineage of party leaders that stretches back more than a century, to before the civil war that swept across China in the late 1940s. In 1949, Communist forces under Mao Zedong took power, with support from the Soviet Union. The defeated Nationalists, led by Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, retreated to their strongholds on Taiwan and a few other islands off China’s coast.

They never acknowledged defeat. Even after Chiang’s death, in 1975, the Nationalists clung to the belief that the Communist regime would eventually collapse, making way for them to retake control of mainland China. The U.S. nurtured that delusion during the first two decades of the Cold War. It opened an embassy in Taipei and treated Taiwan’s leaders as the legitimate government of China. Taiwan even held China’s seat in the United Nations, where Taiwanese diplomats sat behind a nameplate that said China. For its part, the Communist regime in Beijing had no diplomatic relations with the United States or most of its European allies. The U.S. secured its position in Asia through a series of military alliances with China’s local adversaries—South Korea, Japan, the Philippines, and Taiwan.

Taiwan’s status proved untenable. In 1971, the UN gave Taiwan’s seat in the General Assembly to China. Nixon’s visit to Beijing the following year upended American policy toward China and Taiwan. By the end of the decade, the U.S. had withdrawn its embassy from Taipei and opened a new one in Beijing. It had also abandoned its mutual-defense pact with Taiwan and, in its place, provided softer assurances. The Taiwan Relations Act, signed by President Jimmy Carter in 1979, commits the U.S. to continuing to provide “arms of a defensive character” to Taiwan. It states that Chinese aggression toward the island, including an embargo, would be a matter of “grave concern,” whatever that might mean.

This policy of “strategic ambiguity” faced its greatest test during the Taiwan Strait crisis of 1995 and ’96, when the U.S. and China nearly came to blows. The crisis started innocently enough: The U.S. had merely granted a visa for Taiwan’s then-president to speak at Cornell University, his alma mater. China responded to the visit with a series of threats and military exercises, firing missiles in the vicinity of Taiwan and disrupting cargo traffic.

President Bill Clinton, under intense pressure from Congress, sent two U.S. aircraft carriers to the area. One of them, the USS Nimitz, sailed through the Taiwan Strait as a warning to Chinese leaders, who ordered the military to stand down. “They felt a kind of humiliation from that,” Lee Hsi-min, a retired admiral in Taiwan’s navy, told me.

Throughout the crisis, Lee commanded a submarine called the Sea Dragon, which had orders to remain beneath the strait, ready to ambush any Chinese warships that tried to cross. When we met in Taipei this spring, I asked him to describe what he’d felt during those weeks. “I didn’t get scared,” he said. “I was really confident.” The torpedoes he had on board could sink any vessel in China’s fleet, and he had the support of the USS Nimitz behind him. “But now,” Lee said, “I don’t have that confidence at all.”

The Taiwan Strait crisis offered a conceptual blueprint: With enough advanced weapons, Taiwan could hold its own until the American cavalry arrived. China set out to challenge that idea. Within a few years, its defense spending increased by more than 50 percent. The focus was on weapons that could stop American warships from again threatening its shores. By the time Barack Obama took office, in 2009, the Chinese arsenal of submarines and missiles had undermined Taiwan’s defensive strategy.

Arming Taiwan with sophisticated weapons, such as fighter jets and submarines, would not address the imbalance, because China had developed the means to destroy most of them in the opening phase of any war. U.S. military advisers soon began to argue that Taiwan should become a “porcupine republic,” bristling with smaller, portable weapons such as shoulder-fired Stinger missiles. Once properly trained in their use, Taiwanese soldiers would be able to sink enough approaching ships and down enough warplanes to make the idea of an invasion too costly. They could also deploy guerrilla tactics to resist a Chinese occupation.

The new approach quickly gained favor in Washington. But it took another decade to catch on in Taipei. For most politicians, the idea of waging an insurgency in urban areas, with bazooka-toting soldiers on rooftops, does not make for an appealing electoral platform. Inside the military, generals balked at the structural changes needed to prepare for a porcupine defense. It would require giving lower-ranking officers the freedom to act on their own initiative, organizing ambushes and making decisions in a crisis—a foreign notion in their top-down military culture.

When Trump began his first term, in 2017, Taiwan hoped that it might yet acquire the capacity to outgun China through the purchase of high-end American weapons. The U.S. tried to make the Taiwanese military reconsider. “Don’t build the strategy around 300 F-16s,” a U.S. Navy admiral recalls telling his counterparts in Taipei at the time. “This just doesn’t make any sense.” Taiwan could never buy enough jets or warships to rival China’s fleet, he argued: “You need to be able to shoot down aircraft. You need to be able to defeat drones.” (The American admiral, now retired, spoke with me on condition of anonymity because he does business in China.) At that point, China could manufacture more drones than any other country by far. A single company in Shenzhen controls more than 70 percent of the global drone market. Both Russia and Ukraine rely on drone components made in Shenzhen, including the motors, controllers, and batteries needed to fly them.

Taiwan lags far behind in this technology. Not until 2022 did its government decide to form what it calls a national drone team. Taiwan, like the United States, bars the use of Chinese technology in its defense industry. So the team needed to make its weapons from scratch or find alternative suppliers. Max Lo, the founder of a commercial-drone company, was put in charge of the effort, and he began reaching out to contacts in the private sector. It was like Ocean’s Eleven, but with entrepreneurs whose background had little obvious value to the mission. Among the companies Lo recruited was the packaged-food giant I‑Mei, whose cookies and snacks are pantry staples throughout Taiwan. One of its subsidiaries had been working on delivery drones, which qualified the company to join the national drone team. To help get factories up and running, the government offered about $1.5 billion in investments last year, far short of what is needed.

The most successful member of the national drone team has been Thunder Tiger, a publicly listed company that makes dental equipment as well as remote-controlled toys. It began making drones about a decade ago, mostly for use in disaster response. When I visited its headquarters, in the city of Taichung, the general manager, Gene Su, took me on a tour of the factory, in a run-down industrial park. In one room, robotic arms moved around inside plexiglass boxes, spooling copper wires onto little engines that would be used to power drones. The room was no bigger than a three-car garage. To reach it, we passed through a much larger open space, about half as long as a football field, where dozens of people in lab coats sat making dental drills. The company earns most of its money by selling them around the world, Su told me. Drones account for a fraction of its revenue. Taiwan’s defense ministry has said it needs about 200,000 drones. But Thunder Tiger cannot begin to meet those needs without financing from the defense budget. “We’re all just waiting for government money,” Su said. During my visit, I saw some of its designs displayed on a conference table. One, named Overkill, had four small rotors and a fake artillery shell strapped to its belly. It resembled a model I had seen a few months earlier in Ukraine, at a factory in Kyiv that makes about 4,000 small drones a day. At its current capacity, Thunder Tiger would need two months to produce that many.

The U.S. military does not disclose how many troops it has in Taiwan. At a meeting in Taipei, a retired officer in the Taiwanese navy chided me for asking about them. Beijing, he explained, sees any U.S. forces so close to its shores as a provocation. Their mission mainly involves training Taiwanese soldiers on how to use American weapons and preparing them to wage guerrilla warfare.

Mark Montgomery, a retired American rear admiral, has put the size of the U.S. deployment at about 500. “It needs to be 1,000,” he told a congressional hearing in May of last year. “If we are going to give them billions of dollars in assistance, sell them tens of billions of dollars’ worth of U.S. gear, it makes sense that we would be over there training and working.”

Montgomery, who once commanded an aircraft-carrier strike group in the Pacific, belongs to a small but devoted community of Taiwan defenders in Washington. These military veterans and foreign-policy experts still have influence on Capitol Hill. They have little or none in the White House. During the first Trump administration, one of these stalwarts, Matt Pottinger, oversaw China policy on the National Security Council. He worked hard to ensure that Trump’s isolationist urges did not eat away at Taiwan’s defenses. No one seems to play a comparable role in the White House today.

In response to my questions about Taiwan, a senior administration official sent a terse response via email. It focused mostly on contrasting Trump’s positions with those of President Biden, whose name the statement deliberately mangled. “The O’Biden team proved that prioritizing allies’ interests over America’s does NOT result in greater security,” the official wrote.

Biden agreed during his tenure to sell Taiwan about $8 billion worth of weapons, significantly less than the $11 billion Trump has so far approved in this term. But only a fraction of the weaponry has been delivered to Taiwan; the backlog on orders is immense. It would take years for U.S. manufacturers to produce the arms Taiwan has already paid for, especially given the need for them to replenish American stockpiles because of the war in Iran.

In terms of messaging, Biden was far tougher on China than Trump has been. Biden never visited China during his presidential tenure. When asked whether the U.S. military would defend Taiwan, Biden responded on four separate occasions that it would. Trump has never said that. He has focused instead on efforts to do business with China and lower the trade deficit. During his trip to China this spring, Trump invited a coterie of billionaires to join him, including Elon Musk and Tim Cook. A published list of passengers on Air Force One featured Eric Trump and his wife, Lara. But it did not appear to include any recognized China hands. When a veteran of Obama’s National Security Council, Brett Bruen, pointed this out on X, he received a juvenile response from the White House director of communications, Steven Cheung: “Stop calling yourself an expert in anything, aside from sucking.” Cheung added that Bruen was a “slope-brained, mouth breathing moron.”

At least one China expert did join the White House delegation to Beijing: Ivan Kanapathy, the senior director for Asia on the NSC and a Marine Corps veteran. Kanapathy’s views on Taiwan align with those of most other experts in the field, and his writings appear in an influential book, The Boiling Moat, alongside essays by Pottinger and Montgomery. Soon after he joined the White House staff, Kanapathy faced an accusation of disloyalty from one of Trump’s outside advisers, the MAGA influencer Laura Loomer. Ever since then, “he’s barely got a job,” one of his friends, a fellow Taiwan expert, told me. “She’s after him.” (The White House declined to allow Kanapathy to speak with me.)

The expert community often meets up to run simulations of a Chinese attack on Taiwan. The results are almost never reassuring. Over the past three years, the Center for Strategic and International Studies has played out dozens of scenarios in three rounds of war games. The only ones that end in defeat for China have two things in common: Taiwan shows determination in fighting back, and the U.S. swiftly intervenes with the full might of its military. Both must happen. Even then, Taiwan’s infrastructure would suffer weeks of bombardment, while the U.S. and its allies would lose dozens of ships, hundreds of aircraft, and thousands of troops—or so CSIS concluded in the first of three reports about the war games, published in 2023.

Two authors of the CSIS reports, Eric Heginbotham and Matthew Cancian, traveled to Taiwan in 2024 to present their findings to military leaders. They got a mixed reception. One of their meetings nearly ended in a fistfight, Heginbotham told me. In the southern city of Kaohsiung, a group of retired Taiwanese naval officers invited the Americans to an ice-cream parlor and, over a round of sundaes, told them to stop preparing for war. They said that Taiwan possessed neither the determination nor the means to fight, and that the U.S. would never intervene to help. The defeatist attitude angered the two Americans, for what it said about Taiwan’s morale and for a more personal reason: Heginbotham’s son, who serves on a U.S. submarine in the Pacific, could be sent to fight in a war with China. “Sorry for my language, but what the fuck?” he recalled saying. “My son’s life is on the line to defend you guys.”

The circular psychology is hard to break: The U.S. will not step in to help if Taiwan lacks the will to fight, and the Taiwanese will be more tempted to surrender if they believe the U.S. isn’t ready to help them. For most people in Taiwan, the pessimism of the naval officers would not come as a surprise. A survey conducted this spring found that fewer than a quarter of Taiwanese voters consider the U.S. a “trustworthy ally,” and only 35 percent believe the U.S. would be likely to help Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack. Both figures had dropped sharply after Trump began his second term. Among Americans, his claims of friendship with Xi might sound like idle flattery, sly diplomacy, or self-delusion. In Taiwan, they perpetuate the idea that resisting China would be a hopeless cause.

Cheng and the Nationalists now preach this idea in the halls of Parliament. Richard Y. K. Chen, a retired admiral in the Taiwanese navy who represents the party on the defense-and-foreign-affairs committee, told me that Taiwan has no chance of surviving a Chinese invasion even with help from the Americans. He has met with the U.S. military advisers working to turn his country into a porcupine republic, and their plans struck him as fanciful. Once the enemy lands on the beaches, “it’s too late,” the admiral told me. “Even if you try to engage in some guerrilla warfare, the local government agencies have already collapsed.”

The measures he proposed, such as evacuation plans, emergency-medicine distribution, and “societal resiliency to protect the public,” focused mainly on minimizing casualties during a Chinese attack and preserving Taiwan’s infrastructure. When I brought up the Ukrainians, who managed not only to thwart Russia’s attack on Kyiv in 2022 but to partly roll back the invading forces, Chen offered a list of reasons their tactics would not work in Taiwan. Ukraine, for a start, has nearly 17 times more land on which to maneuver, as well as a border with Poland that its allies have used throughout the war for resupply. That would not be possible on an island like Taiwan.

And what about drones? The war in Ukraine has shown their effectiveness, especially for the defenders. The Ukrainians have pioneered the use of naval drones—remote-controlled boats packed with explosives. In the Black Sea, these weapons have helped damage or destroy at least a third of Russia’s naval fleet, forcing the rest of its warships to retreat from their base in Crimea. One of the developers of Ukraine’s most famous naval drone, the Magura, told me it would be particularly useful in the Taiwan Strait, where a few hundred of them could sink a Chinese armada.

Chen gave me a sidelong look when I brought this up, as if to ask whether I could really be so naive. “The Black Sea is not the Taiwan Strait,” he said. For one thing, the Ukrainians have relied on Starlink satellites to pilot their drones against Russia; Elon Musk, who owns those satellites, has not allowed Taiwan to use them. Starlink describes this as a business decision, but many in Taiwan question Musk’s motives, pointing out that his car company, Tesla, has one of its biggest factories in Shanghai. Other satellite networks exist, albeit less reliable ones than Starlink. But Chen brushed those options aside as worthless to Taiwan. Even if Taiwan were to spend many more billions of dollars on advanced weapons, Chen said, “how long can you defend the coast? Three weeks? Four weeks?” In that time, he said, China would already have won.

Given those odds, it did not surprise me to learn that draft-dodging in Taiwan remains pervasive. The government decided only in 2022, after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, to increase the required military service from four months to one year. But the recruitment effort left open a variety of loopholes. Some men of fighting age (19 to 36 years old) have reportedly made themselves obese, eating their way to a medical exemption. Others opted for alternative service. Puma Shen, an ambitious young member of the defense-and-foreign-affairs committee, has campaigned for higher military spending and promoted a culture of respect for the armed services. But when called to complete his own mandatory service, he chose to do it at the transportation ministry, where his work mostly involved giving directions to tourists.

Regular military service in Taiwan also involves a lot of common chores, such as cutting grass, Shen told me in his office in Taipei. “People think it’s a waste of time.” On the wall behind him hung a large poster of David sitting atop Goliath’s severed head. It had been a gift from a soldier he met in Ukraine, which he visited in 2023 to learn from its defenders. The trip made clear how far behind Taiwan’s military had fallen. Only last year did basic training begin to provide lessons in piloting drones rather than fighting with bayonets. Much of the top brass in Taiwan remains averse to risk, change, and new technologies. “They really want to protect their own,” Shen said. “This is the way we always do it.”

The offices of Taiwan’s Parliament occupy a drab building on a narrow street in the center of Taipei. When I arrived one morning this spring, lawmakers had already gathered inside to debate a special military budget. There was no security at the entrance—not even an ID check. A clerk sent me right up to the office of Wang Ting-yu, a senior member of the defense-and-foreign-affairs committee and a close ally of Taiwan’s president.

He happened to be in a meeting with a large U.S. defense firm, AeroVironment, whose representatives sat around his conference table. One of them greeted me as I walked in. We had met earlier that week at a defense forum in Taipei, where he had been talking up the value of an American drone called the Switchblade. Designed to launch out of a tube and explode on impact, the weapon had performed badly against Russian forces in Ukraine. The company has tried to improve its drones based on the lessons from that war. But the U.S. military has reportedly cut back on buying them.

Taiwan can afford a lot of weaponry. Its foreign-currency reserves, the sixth-largest in the world, are worth roughly $600 billion. But a defense bill had been stuck for months in Wang’s committee. Its opponents in the Nationalist Party had turned the budget debate into a proxy battle over Taiwan’s future, its relations with China, and its reliance on the United States. The need for a new budget arose late last year, when the Trump administration approved the biggest sale of American weapons to Taiwan in history. The $11 billion package included rocket launchers, artillery, anti-tank missiles, and other sophisticated gear.

The following week, the Chinese military responded with a series of drills off the shores of Taiwan, firing missiles and rehearsing a blockade. Taiwan’s ruling party used the threats to argue for an additional package of American weapons, this one worth $14 billion. But President Lai needed Parliament to approve all the extra spending. In addition to the annual defense budget, about $20 billion, he sought a special disbursement of more than $40 billion over the next eight years. Roughly three-quarters of it would go toward American arms, while the rest would aid the development of Taiwan’s own defense industry, especially its drone factories.

According to most polls, the extra spending bill had broad support. Voters saw it as a way to deter China and keep the Americans happy. It would satisfy Trump’s demand that all U.S. allies spend more on defense. It would also create jobs in the military industry and stimulate the broader economy, including in districts that the Nationalist Party controls. But the plan faced stiff resistance: In a phone call in February, Xi warned Trump to show “extreme caution.” The White House then decided to withhold the bulk of the arms packages until Xi and Trump had a chance to discuss them in person. Since their summit in May, the sales remain on hold.

For Wang, arms deals double as a test of American resolve. No other country sells weapons to Taiwan. “So it’s a matter of life and death to Taiwan,” Wang said. He did not object to the U.S. pursuing dialogue with China, but he warned that Taiwan must not be used as some kind of bargaining chip. Would Trump treat it like one? Wang looked at his hands for a long moment. “I don’t know,” he said finally. “I don’t criticize our allies.”

In the end, the legislators agreed to a pared-down budget worth about $25 billion. Practically all of it would go toward the purchase of American weapons—the Nationalists managed to cut the money for Taiwan’s drone industry. Nothing was left for the kinds of inexpensive, homegrown systems that Ukraine has used to fight the Russians. In late June, the Nationalists submitted a competing plan to meet the military’s need for drones. It included a lot more oversight and red tape that would slow the process down. Parliament has since been deadlocked over which plan to pursue, leaving the nascent drone program in limbo, which is precisely where China wants it.

After her meeting with Xi in April, Cheng returned to Taiwan with a package of support from the Chinese Communist Party, called “the 10 incentives.” Their provisions would allow Taiwanese farmers, fishermen, and people in some other industries to sell food and goods in China. They also promised that certain TV shows, documentaries, and cartoons from Taiwan would be shown on the mainland (with proper vetting, of course). Chinese state media cast the incentives as a gift from Xi to the Nationalist Party. Friendly behavior, they suggested, would elicit additional favor.

Taiwan’s government has tried to block the incentives, calling them a blatant form of political interference. At the very least, they offered a preview of how the Chinese might try to influence Taiwan’s next presidential election, which is due to take place in 2028. Cheng has suggested that she intends to run, and her campaign will no doubt benefit from the support of China, which she portrays as a generous neighbor. “They have become so modern,” she told me. During her visit to the mainland, officials in Shanghai treated her to an order of bubble tea—a Taiwanese invention—that was delivered via drone. The delegation also attended a performance of Mozart and Tchaikovsky at Beijing’s National Centre for the Performing Arts. “Their chief violinist was actually an American!” Cheng told me through an interpreter. “So I think China has become more confident. They’re more inclusive and more globalized.”

When I asked what China might want in return for its friendly incentives, she seemed surprised at my suggestion that the relationship could come with strings attached. Xi had assured her, she said, that China would respect Taiwan’s system of government. He had not talked about making Taiwan a part of China. He had not brought up the experience of Hong Kong, whose democratic institutions survived for less than a decade after the British colony’s absorption into China in 1997. Wouldn’t China seek to do the same to Taiwan? “No,” she said, using the English word to make sure I understood. “We do not need to sacrifice or make any compromise regarding Taiwan’s freedom, democracy, economy, or our rule of law.”

But China has already worked hard to curtail the rights of Taiwan and its elected leaders. Because of China’s decades-long pressure campaign, only 11 nations have formal relations with Taiwan. In April, China prevented President Lai from visiting one of them: At the request of Beijing, the Seychelles, Mauritius, and Madagascar refused to grant Lai’s plane the right to transit their airspace, forcing him to postpone his trip to Eswatini, a landlocked country in southern Africa. When I asked Cheng about the incident, she shrugged it off, saying Lai had brought it on himself “due to his own policies.”

Last year, a few months after Trump began his second term, his administration denied Lai’s request to stop in the U.S. on his way to Latin America. But Cheng and the Nationalists have faced no restrictions. Less than two months after her visit to Beijing, Cheng led a delegation of party members on a trip to Washington and several other U.S. cities. During an appearance at the Asia Society, in Manhattan, she cast Xi as a reliable partner and repeated her assertion that China and Taiwan belong together. The moderators pressed her to explain how Taiwan’s democracy could survive such a partnership. “It’s a win-win scenario,” Cheng said, recalling how Xi had promised her that “anything can be negotiated.”

In their seats near the front, several experts on Taiwan and retired U.S. diplomats exchanged skeptical looks and rolled their eyes. One whispered to me that Cheng sounded like “a whack job.” To me, she seemed more like an opportunist. At a time of lost trust in American resolve, she has reached for the bargain China is offering. Voters in Taiwan can feel the balance of power shifting, and many will choose the side that looks more stable, even at the risk of their own liberties.

Near the end of Cheng’s talk in Manhattan, a member of the audience stood up and urged her not to pursue this deal. He warned that China would demolish Taiwan’s democracy, as it had demolished democratic processes in Hong Kong, and he demanded to know why Cheng had blocked funding for the drones that Taiwan needs. “Xi Jinping is a dictator!” the man shouted. Security guards then seized his microphone and removed him from the hall. Cheng seemed to enjoy the spectacle. “Drones should not be used as weapons,” she said with a smile, “but they should be used to deliver bubble tea.”

Kinmen island, the westernmost outpost of sovereign Taiwanese territory, used to be a fortress. It sits only a few miles off the coast of China, close enough for a good swimmer to make it across to the mainland. In the late 1940s, the retreating Nationalists built bunkers here, positioned tanks, and studded the coastline with metal spikes to impale enemy landing craft. Thousands of Communist soldiers stormed these beaches during the Battle of Kinmen, in October 1949. Most were killed, the rest taken prisoner.

Today, several monuments commemorate this part of Taiwan’s origin story, and a museum stands near the site of the battle. When I visited this spring, the guides urged me not to miss the immersive experience. It featured a dark room with eerie music and animations of war on the walls. Cameras took my photo and projected it onto a battle scene, inviting me to see myself as a defender of Kinmen. Only a few people alive in Taiwan today can remember fighting a war against China, and the simulation felt like an attempt to help younger generations imagine that experience.

Many schoolchildren come to the museum on field trips. But the more common visitors lately are tourists from mainland China. Ferries bring them to Kinmen several times a day, and local businesses ply them with fried fish and sorghum liquor, the pungent local specialty. Such visits are part of China’s strategy. In a treatise published in 2023, the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party laid out a plan to pamper Kinmen with investment and tourism, turning the island into part of a “demonstration zone” to show what life might be like after the “complete reunification of the motherland.” The plan calls ultimately for a bridge to link Kinmen and the closest city on the mainland, Xiamen, about two miles away.

At the start of his career, Xi Jinping served as the vice mayor of Xiamen. His preferred path for absorbing Taiwan into China has always relied on convincing the Taiwanese that life would improve under Beijing’s rule. China’s growth has made that easier. In the early 1990s, Taiwan’s economy was more than half the size of China’s. Now it’s one-20th the size. Residents of Kinmen can see the skyscrapers in Xiamen. They will soon be able to see jets landing at its new international airport. Many of them feel a greater kinship with the mainland than they do with Taipei.

Atop one of the bluffs closest to China, a tower of speakers still broadcasts Taiwanese propaganda toward the mainland in a loop, calling on the Communists to defect and gain their liberty. The recording used to play loudly enough for people on the mainland to hear it. But local authorities have turned down the volume, converting the speakers into a tourist attraction.

On the beach below, metal spikes still protrude from the sand, tilted at China, eroded by salt water and covered in barnacles. Wooden signs with skulls and crossbones used to warn about the risk of land mines on this coast. But the last of the mines have been cleared away, and the government has declared the beach open for swimming. On my last afternoon on the island, I decided to make my way toward China. My clumsy backstroke carried me 100 yards or so, just far enough to be able to look back at the coast and see that it no longer resembles anyone’s idea of a geopolitical flash point. There were no lookout posts or fortifications, no Taiwanese patrol boats. Only the battle museum and the tower of speakers, playing a message that no one in China can hear.

This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “Will Taiwan Just Give Up?” When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

entries.title: How the Government Wastes Our Time
entries.summary: What do we lose in the hours spent filling out paperwork?
entries.content:
What do we lose in the hours spent filling out paperwork?

Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Americans are bogged down in paperwork for reasons that are sometimes necessary, sometimes thoughtless—and, at times, nefarious. In her new book, The Time Tax: How the Government Wastes Our Time—And How to Fix It, my colleague Annie Lowrey looks at all those hours spent looking for tax documents or trying to certify income for the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, or the FAFSA and finds that things don’t have to be this way.

A time tax is an infliction of “paperwork, effort, delay, and aggravation” that Americans suffer to get the rights they are guaranteed. We have the right to vote in a democracy; a time tax creates obstacles to those rights and makes realizing them cumbersome: They show up as extra identification requirements, when voter fraud is incredibly rare—or, in Jim Crow, as literacy tests.

So many things are easy now. If I get hungry, I can order food from just about anywhere with just a few swipes of my thumb; one click at midnight, and diapers can be at the door before the sun rises. Why is there still such sludge in our bureaucratic systems? On this episode of Radio Atlantic, Annie joins me to discuss how these time taxes show up in our lives and waste our time, and how to make our government more efficient.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Annie Lowrey: I think if instead of saying, This is about the poor people getting this program, or This is about making sure that these programs are secure, we could have a politics that says, This is malign; this is bad policy making. We give the government $8 trillion a year, and it passes back this garbage? No! No.

[Music]

Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris, and today we need to think about all of the ways that the government wastes our time.

I’m only half-joking. If you’ve ever thought to yourself while filling out your taxes or trying to cancel a gym membership that This is taking too long! Don’t they already have this information? There has to be a better way!—you’re not alone.

My colleague Annie Lowrey has a name for these cumbersome processes: She calls them “time taxes.” She wrote about the phenomenon for The Atlantic in 2021, and in her new book, The Time Tax: How the Government Wastes Our Time—And How to Fix It, she explores how and why our time is squandered when it does not have to be.

So, what gets lost in the hours spent filling out paperwork? And how do we fix it?



Annie joins me now to discuss. Annie, welcome to the show.

Annie Lowrey: Thank you for having me, Adam.

Harris: So, I wanna start by talking about the DMV.

Lowrey: Yeah.

Harris: Because, right, it’s Labor Day, government offices are closed, but tomorrow across the country, DMVs are gonna be full of people trying to renew their car registrations, get Real IDs, change their addresses, change their names—whatever it might be.

But those long lines at the DMV, I think, are the most trenchant example of what you call a “time tax.” So what are time taxes, and how do they show up in everyday lives, even outside of the DMV?

Lowrey: So time taxes, these show up everywhere you are encountering the government, and really everywhere you’re interacting with businesses, right? It doesn’t necessarily have to be the government. And a time tax—or what’s called in the academic literature “an administrative burden”—is merely the person who is being bureaucratized, their experience of bureaucracy. So how much work they have to do to apply to something; how much work they have to do to research it; the fees that they might have to pay in some cases; and also their psychological or emotional experience, whether that’s DMV-level frustration or emotional anguish in a welfare program, or even a sense of civic pride that you might get when you’re interacting with a service that makes you feel good about yourself.

Harris: So this is how people sort of interact with different things, right? So like you said, it’s not just the government—it can also be canceling a gym membership. In your new book, The Time Tax, you write about the idea that we see some of the most cumbersome examples of these time taxes as they relate to sort of social-safety-net programs. Food stamps, Medicaid, Social Security—things that people in need of help need to survive.

So why is that? Why do we see a structure where the time taxes seem so cumbersome in those social-safety-net programs?

Lowrey: We see time taxes as a general point, I think, being bigger, more onerous, more expensive in a broad sense of the word for programs that are affecting people with less social status, for whatever reason that might be—people with a history of being discriminated against, people viewed with some kind of skepticism by the state. So that could be people who weren’t born here, immigrants. That could be people with a history of interaction or involvement with the criminal-justice system. That could be different racial groups. White Americans are treated very differently than Black Americans. And absolutely, high-income Americans are treated very different than low-income Americans.

And importantly, I don’t think that’s because low-income Americans are the recipients of this generosity that high-income Americans aren’t. So high-income Americans, they absolutely use programs like Social Security retirement benefits. They use tax programs like the 529 college-savings program or the Home Mortgage Interest Deduction. They benefit from the exclusion of employer-sponsored health benefits in some cases. But we don’t think of those as benefits, right? Those are tax policies—that’s not a benefit. It absolutely is. To the government, in accounting terms, it’s the same thing. It’s just that we’re not asking you to pee in a cup for it, which we do for a lot of benefits where you have to apply and reapply and come face-to-face with a social worker and perhaps fill out forms that might be a hundred pages long. And none of those policies interact with each other; they’re really cumbersome.

And I think that’s because we want to dissuade low-income people from using these, because we believe that some share of them are applying fraudulently. And there’s this thought that, you know, Maybe if you’re low income, you need to get a little bit better at paperwork in your life. You need to straighten up and figure yourself out. And this is an imposition of that moral onto you.

Harris: Yeah, and it’s interesting that you mentioned all the paperwork, and that’s even if they know that the programs exist to help them, right?

Lowrey: Absolutely. Yes.

Harris: And that doesn’t—as you write, that’s not by accident, that historically these sort of cumbersome processes have been used as a form of social control that is as old as data itself.

So can you explain that idea a little bit? That these time taxes aren’t something that popped up in the middle of the 1950s and 1960s with an explosion of bureaucracy.

Lowrey: Absolutely not. So a really clear example of these are the voting rules set out in Jim Crow. They are all hypothetically race-neutral. Or perhaps not all, but mostly, right? They are race-neutral.

But, you know, a poll tax is gonna hit lower-income people, namely Black people, way harder than it’s gonna hit higher-income people. Property rules—if you’re a property owner, that isn’t gonna be applied equally. And something like a grandfather clause is instead going to allow white people, white men, to be able to vote, whereas Black men whose ancestors were enslaved are not going to be able to vote.

And so even now, if we scoot forward, look at some of the rules in the SNAP program, which is food stamps. You can’t buy prepared food with your SNAP benefits. So the rotisserie chickens at Costco or at your grocery store? You cannot get those. Right now, there’s a lot of debate over ensuring that SNAP benefits only go to “healthy food.” So we’re saying, This can only be for nutrition as the state sees it, and we’re worried that you’re buying junk food and eating it.

Never mind the fact, I don’t know, maybe somebody is a runner or a diabetic. Maybe they have reasons to access that. Maybe poor kids should be able to have birthday cakes—that seems fine to me. But that is why it’s a tool of social control. We’re making people know that we are skeptical of their spending habits and we’re attempting to control those spending habits through these little time taxes in the program. And I feel like once you see these, you see them everywhere.

Again, I think it’s actually really good to compare it with the home-mortgage interest deduction that, like, if you have a mortgage, you get it. That’s it. They’re not like, Oh, are you living in a floodplain? Are you designing your home in this way? There isn’t that kind of paternalism in there, where there’s a lot of paternalism in a lot of other benefits.

Harris: During COVID, there were so many programs that were intended to simply help people who were struggling, right? Additional tax benefits and things like that. A lot of those programs were very clearly designed so that they reached the most people with the greatest ease, and they worked. Like the children’s tax credit—things like that worked.

Why don’t we do more things like that?

Lowrey: I think often we have multiple goals in mind with a program. So take TANF, which is the cash-welfare program. Its stated goal, or its original goal, is to end child poverty. TANF as it is currently constructed has no effect on the child-poverty rate, which is remarkable to me. That’s in part because it’s a small program. It’s also because the goal of TANF is to control the behavior of the mostly mothers who are using it. There’s very strict work requirements. If you screw up in TANF, you get sanctioned. You are treated as a fraud risk. You are in trouble in some way. Which is not true—even with the IRS, if you screw your taxes up a bit, they’ll ask for the money or they’ll send you the money if you screwed up in the wrong way. But there isn’t this implication that this was a fraudulent act—unless you’re outright committing tax fraud; I’m just saying if you’ve miscalculated something.

And so this is a way that we shrink public programs, where we’re saying, if we’re looking at the example of means-tested programs, the question is not only, Do you have certain characteristics? Do you fall below a certain income line, taking into account the size of your family and some other things? It’s saying, Okay, but we also need you to be good enough at performing for the state, at filling out this paperwork, meeting with this counselor at this given time.

And it’s just, you know, I don’t know that that’s a really legitimate way to go about it, as opposed to simply saying, Yeah, if you meet the income target, you should have this.

Harris: When we come back we talk with Annie about how to address the time tax.

[Music]]

Harris: So there were about 4 million people in the U.S. when the Constitution was signed in 1787. There are about 350 million people in the country now. And so, as the nation has grown, so has its bureaucracy and the systems that it uses. And over time, those systems age.

It makes sense to want to update them, to want to make them better as technology improves. And at the beginning of the second Trump administration, the president established DOGE, the Department of Government Efficiency; appointed Elon Musk to head it up; charged it with cleaning up the government, modernizing old systems, and making it more efficient. You were working on this book when that began. What did you think of that effort at the time?

Lowrey: A few things. So one was that this was presented as a novel thing. And no, no—there’s, like, more than a hundred years of presidents attempting to do this, saying, The systems have gotten too complicated; we’re gonna clean things up; we’re gonna make the entire system more efficient. So it wasn’t new.

I think that the fundamental idea was a good one. I think that the way that they went about it was, like, I would call it clown college if it weren’t so destructive and cruel. They were just firing civil servants at random. They made all of the federal civil servants send a five-point email explaining what they had done every week.

Harris: Wasting their time.

Lowrey: Yeah, exactly—wasting their time. There was no effort to look at the voluminous reports that we have from inspectors general, for instance, or the government’s various accountability offices to say, Okay, can we actually improve procurement contracts? Or, Could we find out the places where we’re really overspending on something, or, you know, We need some deep improvement. There was none of that.

They hurt service delivery by getting rid of some critical people. They created all kinds of busywork. Not just the [five-point] emails. They slowed things down such that some agencies couldn’t get essential components that they would have needed without the approval of a political operative. So for instance, NASA had to get approval for, like, bolts. I’m pretty sure that NASA knows how to buy bolts, right? That is not the problem with an inefficiency in government. And they never considered the citizen experience. Do we really need to wait this long to vote? Do we have to do our own taxes? We don’t, by the way—the IRS would like to do them for us.

And so it was just this all-out assault on the civil service. And it was the second time that we’ve seen it from President Trump, where he just believes that civil servants are a malign politicized force, that they’re there to take sinecures and draw money away from the taxpayer, when many of them, they just love their work—and they’re actually earning less than they would in private industry—because they’re really dedicated to their jobs and they’re very specialized at what they do.

So, yes, DOGE—good idea. And I hope that that idea carries forward, but I hope that they do it much more effectively and efficiently going around the next time. I’d also note that the great sin of DOGE, too, is that it might end up costing the government money because it caused so many lawsuits. They did so many things without the appropriate permissions, without the legal changes that they needed, that they’ve just been mired in lawsuits.

Harris: So when you say we don’t have to do our taxes. The IRS would like to do our taxes for us? What do you mean by that?

Lowrey: Yes, you have to pay your taxes; you have to do your taxes. What I mean is that nine in 10 American households take the standard deduction, which means that they’re not itemizing their taxes. Generally, it’s because their tax situation is pretty straightforward. And so the IRS has all of the information it needs already to do your taxes for you. They have your payroll data from your employer. If you have a retirement account, they’ll have those financial records from the institution, from your bank or your lender. They’ll have local data as well. So they could merely pre-fill your 1040 for you and send it to you to look over, or they could just send you a summary and say, Okay, if you agree with this, just let us know. You don’t really have to do anything. We’ll send you your refund, or there won’t be any money exchanging hands at all.

And so this is the way that taxes work in a lot of our peer countries with high incomes. In Japan, if you’re earning a salary, for the most part you don’t have to do anything. In some countries in Europe, you can do it all by text message. And the IRS is legally prevented from doing this, such that the average American spends 12 hours a year on the 1040 and spends roughly $300 on tax-preparation services. It’s silly. It’s silly. And there’s some people with very complicated tax situations. Fine. The IRS might have some requests for information. Did you have another kid this year? Did you take out another mortgage? Something like that. But they don’t need these endless, endless, endless, endless forms. They don’t need you to do them or hire somebody else to do them. They could do it.

Harris: To that point, are there other ways that we could be doing things? Is there a better way outside of these time taxes? How can the U.S. make government programs more accessible?

Lowrey: There’s a million and one. And it’s almost—there’s so many options out there that I feel like sometimes it’s hard for me to summarize.

So one straightforward thing is that there are different income standards and eligibility standards that target the same group of people using the same programs, many of whom use multiple programs. So for instance, Medicaid and SNAP—they have different income standards. In some cases, they have different standards of qualifying income, and you can’t cross enroll. So you can’t say, Okay, if I’m eligible for this, then I’ll maybe also be eligible for that. Sometimes that’s because of a difficult reason, so consider jobless insurance, which people often use if they’ve lost their job. That goes to the individual, where SNAP is really aimed at households instead. So that’s actually kind of a technical thing. But just unifying these standards and making such that you could cross-enroll in programs would be a wonderful, wonderful thing to do.

Holding states and offices and DMVs and everything else accountable for counting how much paperwork they’re putting on people, how many people they are not serving or are churning off and on programs because the paperwork is too much, and then saying, Okay, we want you to bring these numbers down—that would be really helpful. We don’t do that.

In terms of health care, dealing with hospitals and insurers and doctors is absolute misery. There’s a lot of common-sense regulation that could prevent health-care providers and insurers from denying procedures that should have been approved, or making sure that your medical bill is actually accurate—which half of them aren’t—preventing them from providing you with what you are paying for through simple paperwork and attrition and frustration, as opposed to some other legitimate tool. So those are just some ideas, but there are a lot out there.

Harris: Well, I guess if there are so many ideas out there, why hasn’t the government used some of those ideas, utilized the modern technology in the same way that, if I wanted a burger right now, I could pull my phone forward and just order it from DoorDash and it’s here in 15 minutes. If I needed a car to get somewhere, it’s, like, two clicks and I’ve got it. We have all of this modern technology. Why haven’t they used that modern technology to streamline a lot of this stuff?

Lowrey: Because the government is not really very good at reforming itself.

A lot of these changes would have to be made by Congress, and Congress doesn’t really care; it doesn’t see itself as a benefits administrator. And we’ve screwed up the lines of responsibility here. So if you’re not getting a benefit that you were supposed to be receiving, who’s at fault? Is that the state administrator? Is that the office that you’re working with, where if you complain, you are concerned that you might be retaliated against? Is that the governor? Is that the president? Because he’s the administrator of the programs, right? Is that Congress?

And I also think that there’s these broken feedback loops, by which I mean: If you get Social Security retirement benefits, we have decades of beautiful political-science research showing that it makes you feel like a citizen; it makes you feel like a good person; it makes you more likely to vote; it makes you more likely to be civically engaged in lots of ways. And seniors, when there are threats to Social Security, they come out and they demand that politicians stop it.

But there’s so many other little, tiny problems that relate to other programs that I don’t think that we have a mass politics demanding this. And so that’s why I think it’s hard. Nevertheless, when politicians do this stuff and make things easier, I think often it goes really well. It’s been really popular for, for instance, Zohran Mamdani in New York City. And I think that to a certain extent, we’re still operating under this understanding that these administrative burdens are demanded by the broad public because they’re so afraid of fraud in these programs. But there’s not that much fraud in these programs. We have really good ways to detect it. Giving more money to the civil service such that they could stamp fraud out would be a way to do it. And I just, I don’t know that people are voting on the basis of the way that the IRS is administering audits to other taxpayers. I don’t think that they are.

Harris: I mean, they might be.

Lowrey: Some of it. Everybody’s voting for something.

Harris: About the sort of weaponization of data that we’ve seen over the last year and a half, and the counterargument to The government should do more things to make lives better with our data is that the government can also take our data and do things that are nefarious if they so chose to, right? You can look at the Stasi; you can look at the Pinochet regimes.

How do you balance those concerns? Or does the government just already have so much data that they don’t necessarily factor in?

Lowrey: I think it’s a real concern and a real threat, since we are in an environment of democratic backsliding. This is one of the reasons that mixed-status families with citizen children and perhaps undocumented parents don’t get safety-net benefits that they have every right to get. That kid is a citizen; they’re allowed to get it. It’s because they don’t want to invite this state that could be very threatening to them into their lives.

I think one way to think about this is to give Americans the choice and to give the government permission: Okay, if I want this benefit, I feel comfortable with this office getting my data from the IRS. Something like that, so that it is elective and so that people can decide.

Harris: You point to Estonia in the book as a sort of prime example of a place that’s successfully easing the administrative burden on their citizens. But you also mentioned that they’re a small country. And as you were talking about, the gargantuan task of making the systems talk to each other in the United States, it makes me think that we have a scale problem here, that we might just be too big to eliminate some of the cumbersome bureaucracy. But how do you square the Estonian example with our context in the U.S.?

Lowrey: Yeah, Estonia is something we can aspire to, but I don’t think it’s ever gonna be something that we’re gonna have. So the thing about Estonia is they build a completely new government after they break away from the Soviet Union and regain their independence.

So Estonia regains its independence in the summer of 1991, and they form a government completely de novo, from scratch, at that point. And they do so during a climate where they want Estonians to trust the government because so many didn’t due to the Soviet influence.

And so they create the most elegant system of benefits that are all controlled by an ID number on all of these databases that are designed and updated constantly to talk to each other, such that Estonia has this policy that if you tell the government, any part of the government, a piece of information about yourself once, everything updates.

So for instance, if you tell the voting authority, My address has changed, all of the hospitals know it. All the schools, everything knows it. All of your mail goes to your new address. It’s nothing like that in the United States at all. So I don’t think that we are gonna become that—again, a very small homogenous country that started in the 1990s functionally. But I think that we can become more Estonia-like. And they’ve also had some issues with data security. They take it really seriously. So maybe there’s some lessons from Estonia to us, too, about setting these systems up in a way that is secure.

Harris: What would it take to implement some of those ideas from there? Is this just a political-will question?

Lowrey: Yeah, I do think it is a political-will question. And I think it’s a political-framing question. Because very often, administrative burdens are framed as necessary to prevent fraud. They’re not terribly good at preventing fraud. They’re much better at preventing people from getting needed benefits. But I think if instead of saying, This is about the poor people getting this program, or this is about making sure that these programs are secure, we could have a politics that says, This is malign; this is bad policy making. We give the government $8 trillion a year, and it passes back this garbage? No! No. Right? At least do the obvious stuff here.

And I also think that there’s ways of thinking about new policy changes that could be administratively light. So for instance, there’s always been this idea to put children up to the age of 18 on Medicare, which comes and goes and comes and goes. That’s a nice thing to do because it would mean that just kids are on Medicare. You never have to worry if your kid gets a broken bone or, God forbid, a cancer, that they’re always gonna be able to get treatment. But more than that, it’s just elegant. It’s simple. It’s the government taking work away from you.

I think about this a lot in terms of free school meals as well. That’s not only a benefit for lower-income families that might be having nutritional challenges. It’s also like, If you don’t have food in the house just because you forgot, oh great, the school’s just gonna feed your kid and you don’t have to worry about it. It’s just a nice thing in terms of reducing those burdens.

And so I think that a lot of that could be really popular. One thing I think about a lot is: We focus so much on reducing unnecessary burdens on businesses. Can we think about it in terms of reducing unnecessary burdens on families? Whether that’s these insurers that are not really insuring us, or this tax authority that makes us do our own taxes, or any other program where it’s just hard to grapple with.

Harris: Annie, here is to hoping that that burden is alleviated. Thank you so much for joining.

Lowrey: Thank you. I do hope. Thank you so much, Adam.
